maintopic: DEATH OF MR. T. H. THOMPSON, M.P.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEATH OF MR. T. H. THOMPSON, M.P.
speechtext:
It is only a fortnight
since mention was made in this House of the death at Ottawa of one of its hon. members from the province of Quebec. To-day it is our sad duty to record the loss of another hon. member, Mr. Thomas Henry Thompson, member for East Hastings in the province of Ontario.
Mr. Thompson's death occurred with tragic suddenness. Though not in the best of health, he was to all appearances hale and hearty when the House adjourned over the week end on Friday last. On Saturday morning, due, it is thought, to over-exertion, he suffered a heart strain from which he rallied' for a brief time, but within twenty-four hours he had passed away.
Mr. Thompson was in his fifty-ninth year. He was first elected a member of parliament in 1917, at which time he was returned as the Conservative member for the constituency of East Hastings. He was reelected in the general elections of 1921. Prior to his entry into federal politics he had1 taken an active part in the municipal affairs of his native township and county. He was reeve of Madoc village on more than one occasion, and for five years was member of the Hastings county council. In 1913 he was chosen warden of the county.
His business and commercial interests, especially as a manufacturer and buyer of cheese, gave Mr. Thompson a special knowledge of many branches of agriculture. For ten years he was a director of the Eastern Ontario Dairymen's Association and for three years he was president of the Madoc Agricultural Society. The knowledge thus acquired he turned to the advantage of all concerned, as occasion arose for the consideration of agricultural problems in this House. Mr. Thompson did not take much part in debate. Like the hon. member for Compton who predeceased him, he was one of those members who make their presence felt by the faithfulness of their attendance in the House but whose influence is not less great because so largely silent and unobtrusive.
Hon. members on this side will join with me in extending to my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) and those who sit about him, our sympathy in the loss of one who was a highly respected member of the Conservative party. May I ask, Mr. Speaker, that irrespective of party, you will convey to Mrs. Thompson and her daughters, on our behalf, expression of the sympathy felt for them in their great bereavement by all hon. members of this House.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DEATH OF MR. T. H. THOMPSON, M.P.
speechtext:
It was a distressing shock to myself to hear yesterday morning by telephone of the death of one of our colleagues in this group in the House, all the more so because I had personally no intimation that Mr. Thompson suffered from any disability. His closer companions amongst us were aware that for some time he had been afflicted, as was thought in a minor way, with weakness of the heart, but unaccompanied, so far as anyone knew, with any serious apprehensions as to his life. The suddenness of it all was the greater because within a few hours before, he had mingled with his fellow-members here, apparently in the best of spirits and of health.
The Prime Minister has reviewed Mr. Thompson's association with this parliament and, as well, has made mention of those things in which he had engaged prior to his entry here. Any office of civic honour that he did not fill was not within the reach of the man. He appeared to have freely gained and very long sustained the unbounded confidence of his fellow-citizens; and if a knowledge of the affairs of a constituency, an intimate acquaintance with all its activities, close, indeed familiar, information as to each and all of those whom he represented, constitute the best attributes and qualifications for a member of parliament, Mr. Thompson would in-

Questions

deed be hard to excel. There was nothing of value to the people of his riding that he did not understand as well or better than they, and he seemed to consider it his one duty here to reflect the mind of his people on all questions of public import. Nor was there anything that his industry did not apply itself to that he felt would be of value to those whom it was his privilege to serve. He enjoyed, as well, and of us still more emphatically, the affection of his fellow-members of parliament. Modest in demeanour, as modest as his career was creditable to himself, unobtrusive on the floor of the House, but ever at hand to serve, he gained the esteem of and finally became beloved by all.
It is with very, very deep feeling indeed, that I ask that we all do join in the message which you have been kindly deputed to send to his widow and daughters.

maintopic: DEATH OF MR. T. H. THOMPSON, M.P.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the members who sit in this part of the House, may I add a few words to what has been said? The death of Mr. Thompson came with startling suddenness; he had1 done his day's work and has been called home-a striking reminder to all of us of the uncertainty of human life. As has been said, Mr. Thompson was a man who took an active interest in public life and had rendered great service to his community before he came to this House. I was not intimately acquainted with him, but judging from what I saw and what I know, I think that to know him was to love him. I am sure he was held in the highest esteem and respect by those who were intimately associated with him. Undoubtedly he was respected by all the members of this House. I hope, Sir, that you will convey to his wife and daughters our sincere sympathy in the great loss which they have sustained. May his memory be to them a comfort and a joy, that he was a good father, a good husband, and a good public servant.

1.	How many officials of the Canadian National Railways receive as remuneration $10,000 or more per year?
2.	What is the total amount paid by the Canadian National Railways, in salaries or other remunerations which amounted in each case to $10,000 or more per year?

Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend (Mr. Doucet) can hardly be serious in pressing this same question again. Already this session several questions along the same lines have been asked, and in the interests of the Canadian National Railway Board, and on their advice, I have declined to answer them.
On February 23 my hon. friend himself asked these questions:
1.	How many officials of the Canadian National Railways are in receipt of a salary of $10,000 and over per annum ?
2.	What are their names?
I replied:
This is a question similar to others asked and which, in the interest of the Canadian National Railway Board, it would not be in the interest of the railway to make public.
I like to give all the information asked for, but this is a matter of business in which the people of Canada, through the Canadian National Railway Board, are endeavouring to carry on a commercial enterprise under great difficulties. The question refers absolutely to operation, and I think we have pretty well established the principle that matters affecting operation only should be very carefully handled when information is asked for. True, perhaps I fell from grace in this connection when the other day the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) asked about salaries over $15,000. Now, to show the House that I had in mind on that occasion the idea of guarding against the appearance of just such a question as this, perhaps I may be permitted to read what I said. The question was:
1.	How many officials or officers of the Canadian National system receive salaries or remuneration amounting to $15,000 per year or over?
2.	What was the total amount paid by the Canadian National system for salaries or other remuneration amounting in each case to $15,000 per year or more in the year 1924?
This is the answer I gave:
Mr. Speaker, this is a peculiar question in that it seeks to have the Canadian National Railways give to the public information which no other railway company gives. It really is asking the railway owned by the government to do something that no other railway company in Canada is asked to do, or does, or, possibly, would do. I may say this, however. The management of the Canadian National Railways are very much averse to giving this information, for the reasons I have suggested. I have urged them to give it in this case, particularly as it relates only to the higher paid officials and does not include the employees in general. With that understanding-that it is not opening the door to a series of questions that will be handing the entire information as to salaries over to the public for use by other companies, information which if given would also give rise to endless jealousies in the staff itself-I am prepared to answer the question. The answer being confined within the limits I have stated, I do not think it will do any appreciable harm.
So I think the answer to the question asked to-day, Mr. Speaker, will have to be that the Canadian National Railway Board are fully convinced that it would be detrimental to the interests of the operation of the great national railway undertaking to give out such information as this, which, of course, would only lead to other questions of a similar character; and I agree with the management in that view.

Before my hon. friend finally disposes of the matter, I would ask him to be kind enough to read the evidence of Sir Henry Thornton on this point before the special committee of the House the other day. He was asked what would be the disadvantage of giving such information as this, and the gist of his reply-I am not giving the exact words, but I think my hon. friend will find that I am right in stating the gist of it-was that it would not be nice for employees to have their salaries talked about; it would not be nice to have it known that they were working so cheaply.

The minister says there
has been a total reduction in the permanent staff in four years of 49; but I do not understand that- there has been any corresponding reduction in the amount of the salaries paid. Will the minister kindly inform me what the reduction, if any, has been in the total cost of the inside and outside service in the same period of time?

According to the figures

Since the work of the department has been reduced to an almost negligible quantity, is it the intention of the minister to cut down the staff still further? I am informed by militia officers that the vote passed by parliament is so small-and I think the minister will agree with the statement- that very little useful work can be done among the militia units in the Dominion. If that be the case is it not possible to reduce the cost of the overhead of this department? Personally I have a good deal of sympathy with the department, and I should like to see it placed in a position to carry on its work properly; but inasmuch as parliament in its wisdom has not seen fit to grant the minister the necessary money to do that, I think the overhead should be cut down. What are the views of the minister on the subject?

It is in the interest of the country that the department should be maintained in such a position that if the necessity arose we could adequately perform our duty to the nation. With regard to the question of expenditures for these various services, (he permanent force has been decreased to a certain extent in numbers, but we are preserving it in a fairly good position. As to votes for militia services outside, these have been cut down to a very great degree. However, it has been represented to me, particularly by those who are interested in the maintenance of the artillery service throughout the country, that as a result of the economies which the department has put
into effect that force has become paralysed practically, owing to its inability to obtain that training with the guns which is essential to maintain it in proper order. I have received letters from a great number of members of parliament in regard to that subject, and I would be very glad to know what the sense of the House is on that question. I am sure the House will agree that it is the duty of Canada, like every other country, to maintain its military and naval establishments in such a condition that if it became necessary for the defence of our own interests those establishments could be expanded. Just now when taxation is being imposed upon the country to a greater degree than ever before in Canadian history I am one of those who think that, while we should maintain our organization, it is not proper to ask for large amounts of money from this House or to impose further burdens upon the people. At the same time I am not one of those who think that sweet peace is likely to be permanent. My visit to Europe last year and to the League of Nations impressed me most forcibly with the fact that at any time a condition may arise in Europe which will bring about another conflagration, which, while it might probably not be as great as the unfortunate war which broke out in 1914, would nevertheless involve a great many nations. For that reason I think we should maintain our organzation.

In view of the minister's
statement that there is always a possibility of further conflagrations, not only in Europe but the world over, why is proper provision not made for the units in this- country to carry on at the present time? I think there are something over 250 units which receive for their annual training and administration sums not in excess of $2,000, and are required to find out of their own pockets anywhere from $6,000 to $10,000 a year to enable them to carry on.

I rise to a point of
order. I believe we are discussing civil government estimates, and the remarks of my hon. friend would not come under the head of civil government.

speechtext:
I draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that civil government items deal with everything relating to the policy of the department. It is the one vote that is most general in its character and under that vote practically everything relating to the department or to the policy of the department may be dealt with. It is the one item that may be called really general.
Supply-Defence

I am not discussing at this
moment the general policy. I am asking the minister, in view of his own statement of the possible dangers that confront the country, why does not the country make proper provision for the training of the units which it has authorized and which are organized in the country? Why does the country ask those commanding officers to contribute their own funds? Why will members of parliament support a policy which makes it necessary for individuals to contribute out of their own pockets four times the amount this country contributes for their training?

I am well
aware of the great sacrifices which are being made from year to year by the officers of the militia forces. They carry on .these organizations at great expense to themselves with very.great unselfishness and patriotism. That is a matter which is not fully realized throughout the country generally. Anyone who has had to do with the administration of this * department, or who knows anything about dealing with these questions, knows that my hon. friend is right in his statement as to the unselfish conduct of the militia officers. As to how much they spend in comparison with the amount of this vote I am unable to say exactly; but I know they have been very generous in helping to maintain the militia. So far as the infantry is concerned, we are able to maintain that organization, and to give a number of days' training under the vote which we have in the estimates, but I confess that I think the situation with reference to the artillery service requires consideration. That service developed tremendously during the late war, and the officers con-
4 p.m. nected with the service throughout the country generally are splendid men, who took a very great interest in the extremely technical work that is necessary to be mastered in order to become efficient military officers; and the representations which have been made to me with reference to the position of that force are to the effect that, in consequence of the limited amount of money that we have been able to devote to the maintenance of the artillery, there is danger that these corps in certain portions of the country will have to disband. I am considering the question of placing in the supplementary estimates an amount to deal with this matter. However, every minister who is responsible for the administration of affairs to-day experiences great difficulty when requests come in from various portions of the country with regard to what seem to be very necessary- and important matters, inasmuch as [The Chairman, [
we necessarily hesitate when we come to consider the fact that all this money must be obtained1 by taxation; for the burden of taxation upon the people of the country to-day is very great, and every proposition must be approached with a full regard for the responsibility involved in the expenditure of every dollar of public money. That is the way I feel in regard to administering this department, although I would be anxious, if it were possible, to spend further sums.

I think there are many governmental departments where economies can be carried out and less expenditure made at the present time; but I make one exception, and that is the Department of National Defence. I do not think we can reduce expenditure in this department and still maintain a reasonable efficiency. On the contrary, I think that this department has reached the stage where less money is being spent upon it than is really in the public interest. The defence of the country is just as necessary, or perhaps more necessary, than any other feature of governmental work. The minister has asked for an expression of opinion regarding the training of the artillery. We are aware that men all over the country have been urging that sufficient opportunity be given for artillerymen to receive their training. It is not a training that can be acquired in a short period; it is a skilled department of the militia which requires to be kept up by regular practice and in sufficient numbers. I believe that if an adequate vote is not provided for the artillery in the end the country will suffer. So far from being an excessive expenditure, if the vote is not passed it will be a serious loss, because we will lose those men who have had training and those men who may now receive the training in the future, which will leave us in an inferior position. I believe the minister will receive generous support if he sees his way clear to increasing the allowance for the artillery. While I speak in this way in reference to artillery, I am speaking also generally. While care and economy should be practised in all departments, I do not see how we can reduce the number of men receiving annual training at the present time.

I desire to add a word
to what has been stated by the hon. member for St. John and Albert (Mr. MacLaren). In the province of New Brunswick during the last few months the artillery officers are very keen about the service and nearly every one of them was a returned war veteran; they are all desirous of seeing that branch of the service kept up to the proper level. If I

Supply-Defence
recollect aright, they passed a resolution, the effect of which was that unless there was some further appropriation for the service it would be impossible for them to carry on, and I was among those to whom this resolution was sent. I had the honour of forwarding it to the Minister of National Defence. I believe it was received sympathetically by the minister, and I hope he will be able to place something in the supplementary estimates, as he has indicated, in order to do something for the artillery. I think this branch of the service should not be lost sight of. It is just as important-perhaps more so, especially along the coast-as the infantry branch of the service, and I think that in following the course indicated by the hon. memlber (Mr. MacLaren) the minister will have the support of the best sentiment of the people.

I shall say just a few words
in support of what the minister has stated as to the need of the artillery. If the artillery does not get support we might as well dispense with it; and in making these remarks I want to appeal to hon. members, especially those who believe that we should be prepared at all times to defend our country and that if the time ever comes, misfortune though it might be, for us to fight again, we shall have the courage to do just as we did before. I appeal to these hon. members because the defence forces of Canada are in a pitiable condition. The minister has stated that there is need to give further support to the artillery, and I agree with him; if you do not supply the artillery with the ammunition with which to practise then it is hopeless to expect to train an efficient force in that branch. The minister also stated that there was provision for the infantry. Well, I know of my personal knowledge that there is not provision for the infantry; there is provision for the training of one hundred men in each unit in the infantry, but that is not sufficient. Such provision is just sufficient to discourage officers and non-commissioned officers whn are capable of training men; it will only serve to diminish the interest they take in the defence forces, to dampen their ardour, and to make them feel like quitting.
It was the infantry I had in mind particularly when I said that the officers of the units in Canada had to go down into their own pockets, or to depend upon public support, to get the money that is necessary for their training. I have somewhere among my papers, and I shall be glad to give it to the minister, a detailed statement showing the annual expenditures, absolutely cut to the bone after
various consultations, in a militia unit in the city of Vancouver. In that particular unit, the sum required annually amounts to $8,000. And they receive $2,000 from the country with which to carry on. That sort of thing is hopeless. The training of one hundred men is not sufficient. I am not personally identified with any unit in Canada, being now on the reserve; so that I have no axe to grind for any particular organization. But I know the condition that exists; I have gone into it carefully.
Let us reflect for one moment on the advantage it would be to us to have a thoroughly trained body of men if the defence forces of Canada were ever called upon again to go to war. In the Great war, while the Canadian forces were given credit for having done almost impossible things-and they did do almost impossible things-it was not until late in 1916, over two years after the outbreak of war, that the Canadians were able to put a complete corps in the field and fight as a unit from Canada. If we had not been dependent on the Mother Country and the Allies, what sort of war would Canada have fought? We should have been crushed before we started. Now, as a result of training, casualties can be avoided; on the other hand, owing to lack of proper preparation, every force that went into the field not thoroughly trained suffered casualties untold. A comparison might well be made between the Canadians, after they were able to fight as a unit, and the Americans who came into the field, much as we entered in the early stages, inexperienced and untrained. If hon. members will make the comparison between the accomplishments of the two forces under such conditions they will find that the achievements of the Canadians in the last hundred days of the war were almost as great as those of the Americans, despite the fact that the latter had, I suppose, ten times our force. And this was due to the experience which the Canadians had gained through training and discipline.
With a backbone in Canada to-day of officers and non-commissioned officers of experience, the foundation can be laid for a defence force which, with very little training, could take the field in case of emergency. But if we allow the force to go to pieces, as it is unquestionably doing to-day, then should another war occur Canada would enter it much in the same condition as she entered the last ,war. And, proud as we may be of the showing which this country made in that war- and undoubtedly individual battalions and individual divisions did admirably-it is

nevertheless lamentable that as a unit Canada was unable to make a showing within a period of two years. The only way therefore that Canada can prepare herself for any similar emergency is to give proper and decent support to her defence forces.
Furthermore, the cost will not be much. To-day the vote for annual training is something like $1,000,000, and if that were increased to $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 a great deal could Ibe done towards the efficient training of the forces. It has been said that taxation is severe. I agree; and I think that we could find innumerable places where the expenditures could be cut down or perhaps done away with altogether. We are voting money for grain elevators and railways in connection with which, iwith careful consideration, we might save many millions. But when it- comes to something for our own defence then we are apathetic, we are not very enthusiastic about our duty. The first duty of every man is to his country; and this is the opportunity to do something to show that our hearts are right.

Where would the hon.
member suggest cutting down grain elevators?

I have not suggested any
place in particular nor have I specially looked into that matter. I am not discussing the question of any particular grain elevator, although my own city is vitally interested in grain elevators. I mentioned this as something which I should probably advocate for my own city. But I do not care whether it be grain elevators or railways or anything else; if you look over the estimates you will find from beginning to end innumerable places where you might reduce them by millions. And I say that this is one direction in which neither Canada nor any other country can afford to be niggardly. At a recent dinner a Canadian officer was deploring the very condition which I am now deprecating; he referred to "O Canada!" and he said something like this-"O Canada! We stand on guard for thee-at a lower capital cost than that of any other country in the world except Bolivia." That is the record of Canada, and it is something that is most lamentable if we are really patriotic and desire to see our young men trained so that in case of emergency they may be able to defend their country.

Mr. Chairman, you have just
stated that this is the opportunity we should take to discuss the general policy of Canada with regard1 to military affairs. I do not think there is any difference of opinion in this 
House as to the desirability of defence, but there may be all the difference in the world in our opinion as to what is the best means of defence. I would suggest to hon. members that before we get too far into the subject we should1 give very serious consideration to the basic question-as to whether or not after all, we are better defended by being defenceless in the ordinary acceptation of that term. Even if we admit-which I do not-that the best method of defence is by naval or military preparations, there are all kinds of such preparations that might be considered defensive. Reading a pamphlet issued by the Navy League some little time ago I noticed a statement to this effect:
From the point of view of Canada, we may as well put the idea of invasion out of our heads. It does not enter into the question. But the protection of trade should indeed receive most careful and studied consideration by both people and parliament.
I cite that merely to show that even this league, which stands for active defence by physical means or armaments, argues that Canada does not need to consider the danger of invasion. If that is admitted, it makes a great deal of difference in our discussion of what would be the best method of defence.

Just what difference does it
make ?

I do not know that I am
called upon to answer that question, but it certainly would make a great deal of difference. For instance, if there were no danger of invasion we would not need to have, as I take it, a large army.
Does my hon. friend suggest that we have a large army?

I do not suggest that we have or that we ought to have. I simply rose, Mr. Chairman, to draw the attention of the House to the propriety of deciding in our own minds as to what after all is the best kind of defence. Later on in the debate I ,may have something to say on that question, but now I merely submit that it is a basic question, and before we make assumptions it seems to me we ought to be certain that those assumptions are at all events tenable and to some extent justifiable.
There is another subject, Mr. Chairman, which I should like to see discussed, but I am not sure whether this is the proper time to bring it to the attention of the House.
I have recently received a very interesting, indeed a startling pamphlet, written by John S. Ewart, entitled "Canada and the Next War." It contains statements as to the present position of Canada and her obligations which I think are of paramount importance.

May I ask the hon. gentleman whether he agrees with the expressions of opinion in that pamphlet?
I am not discussing the contents of the pamphlet for the moment, Mr. Chairman.

Could the minister give us information as to the number of men who are to receive annual training this year; the number who were trained in 1913, the year before the war; and similar figures for an intermediate year, say, 1920?

It would be more advantageous if my hon. friend would wait till we come to the item particularly relating to the militia. My officers tell me they have not the information going back that far, but I will get it for my hon. friend.

I want it merely for
purposes of comparison.
Yes.

Mr. Chairman, the military
men have had their innings in discussing this question. It seems to me that perhaps the military mind does not always view it just exactly the same as the civilian mind does. Sixty thousand Canadians laid down their lives in "a war to end war." I want that phrase to sink into the minds of hon. members to my right, who have been talking about the "next war"-sixty thousand Canadians laid down their lives in a war that was to end war; now we are busily talking about how we are going to raise another big army to go to war again. Just as long as we have discussions of this kind in every country under the sun we will have war. If we spend our time on the problems of peace, spreading the gospel of peace and showing how peace can be brought about, we will accomplish a great deal more in preserving peace than we can ever expect to by talking about preparing for war. Whom are we going to go to war against I want to know? Who are our enemies? Where is the hostile force that is hovering on the borders of this Dominion ready to attack us if we have not a large army to defend ourselves?
May I ask a question?
A dozen, if you please.

Did my hon. friend or any
other human being in the world know whom we were going to war with in 1914?

We had a pretty good idea.
From what we read in the newspapers for years preceding 1914 we knew that military preparations were being made on a large scale, that in fact Europe was an armed camp, and that war was bound to come.

Does my hon. friend recall
the Prime Minister of Great Britain announcing in the Imperial House of Commons not more than a week before war broke out that there was no danger of war?

Did you ever see a small
boy with a toy who did not want to use it? Military men are just grown up boys, and they want to see how their "toys" will work, they want to use them. Those in control of huge armies want to try them out. Canada is the most happily situated of any country in the world to teach the uselessness of war.
Mr, CLARK: Did the British Empire want to try its army out?
I do not wish to carry on a dialogue with my hon. friend.

You invited me to ask a
dozen questions. Having asked only three,
I have another nine still coming.

I believe it is quite right
to have a skeleton army of the smallest possible size to take care of any internal disorders that may break out, and to do its share if the country is ever attacked, which I think is a very remote contingency. I believe that if we attend to our own business and keep the banner of peace unfurled there is very little danger for a long time to come of this Dominion being invaded. I have every respect for hon. members to my right who were engaged in the late war and realize the dangers resulting from national unpreparedness, I have also considerable sympathy for their trend of thought. But, Mr. Chairman, I sincerely believe that if we talk peace, prepare for peace, and look for peace, we will get peace; and I am convinced that if we talk war, prepare for war, and look for war, we will get war. I would cut this vote down to the lowest possible minimum, just continuing our present forces without enlarging them to any extent whatever. It seems to me that if we had twice as much money to spend just exactly the same arguments might be brought forward by hon. gentlemen to my right in favour of a still larger expenditure. What is " adequate protection "?-to use a phrase familiar in tariff matters. One member might answer, a force of a hundred thousand men, while another would be con-
Supply-Defence

tent with fifty thousand men, and so on. There never will be any concrete idea of what actually constitutes adequate protection in a military sense. We cannot compete with the great military nations, neither could we defend ourselves against them. Personally, I have sufficient faith in human nature to believe that if we attend to our own business and, as I said before, look for peace, we will get peace. I would not be in favour of augmenting this vote by one single dollar.

The hon. member for
Brandon has entirely misapprehended the argument advanced by members of this group. No one suggests that Canada should maintain a large standing army. Such a thought was not expressed here this afternoon or at any other time, and it is not fair to suggest that that was the argument we put forward. What we have suggested is this: Canada is spending less per capita to-day upon national defence than any other civilized country, and the minister's own remarks bear out the statement that has been made throughout the country that the vote is so small that it is not possible to maintain even the skeleton service that is required in the case of the artillery. Artillery officers who have put their hands in their pockets year after year to provide funds since this vote was reduced to such slender proportions are getting tired of this sort of thing. I wonder if the hon. member himself is satisfied that militia officers, men of high standing in his own province and in other provinces, should be obliged to contribute from their own private funds in order to ensure the existence of a skeleton force. Artillery officers in my own province tell me they are going to abandon the whole thing if they do not get enough money to enable them to train at least once in two years a sufficient force of men to keep the skeleton organization going. We have not even got that, and that is all anybody is asking for. I do not think the hon. member is doing himself justice or that the patriotic people of Manitoba will back him up if they understand exactly what the situation is and what hon. gentlemen in this comer of the House are asking for.

Has the minister considered a proposal originating from the Air Force Club of British 'Columbia with regard to the establishment of a reserve air arm by way of supplementing the existing Royal Canadian Air Force? The proposal is contained in a resolution adopted by the club and forwarded by Major Bell Irving, its president, to members of the House and to the minister. 
The gentlemen making this suggestion are competent by experience and by training to express an opinion of value on the question, and I would be interested if the minister could tell the committee whether the proposal is considered to be a practicable one and whether it will be gone ahead with.

The suggestion that came from Vancouver through Major Irving has been submitted to the officers of my department having to do with the air force. I shall be glad to bring down, when we come to the vote for air services, the memorandum which was submitted to me in that connection.

I do not wish to plead for any waste of money, but I want to make a suggestion to help the minister to prevent the waste of money. If you go below a certain point in the training of artillery it would be better, I think, to abandon it altogether, because what you do is nothing but a waste of time and money. As my hon. friend (Mr. Hanson) has said, artillery officers in his province have contributed pretty largely of their private means in connection with the work of the artillery unit. They do that for certain purposes in connection with training, but they cannot do it to the extent of providing shells, and an artillery unit that is trained without actual experience in firing at a target is not worth keeping up. This material must be supplied, otherwise the whole scheme is abortive. The artillery officers are saying that it would be far better to drop the whole thing than to give them so little that they cannot produce any effective results. I would like to quote from a letter I received on this subject from a very enthusiastic artillery officer who took part in the South African war and in the Great war as well. He says:
The portion of the national defence vote allotted to the training of the entire artillery forces of Canada for 1924 was approximately $57,000, and a similar meagre expenditure is proposed for the coming year. An amount of $400,000 was voted in 1924 to cadet corps work.
I am not criticizing the vote for the cadet corps, but if we are to have any talk about militarism and the old cry of " Shall I train my boy to be a soldier," it would be far better to direct such comments to the activities of the cadet corps than to the artillery, which must be a necessary part of Canada's protective force if we are to have any force at all as a part of the force which must be called upon for immediate duty if anything happens. My friend says further:

Though the militia officers appreciate the value of such training, it does appear as a most disproportionate amount in view of that expended on artillery. The training for last season, which is proposed for the coming season, is, in the unanimous opinion of all commanding and senior officers, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, absolutely inadequate to maintain the esprit de corps and efficiency of the Canadian artillery. It is the serious belief of such officers, and the unanimous opinion of the Canadian Artillery Association that should such training not be improved upon, it would be better to cease training altogether, until such time as sufficient training grant can be obtained.
Then he points out that the Canadian Artillery Association, at its annual meeting on the 26th of February last, embodied these views in a resolution, which, I have no doubt, has been communicated to the minister. He is of the opinion that an additional sum of not less than $200,000 is required to train the batteries as they were trained in 1923. A large part of the money is not only for material but for transportation charges, and those transportation charges largely go to the Canadian National Railways. I have no doubt that the minister has had this matter brought before him repeatedly from many quarters and that the representations put forward have met with his personal sympathy. I think his real difficulty is to convince the representatives of the people that it is worth while to do something for this particular branch of the service.
I want to ask the attention of the committee to a matter very far removed from the one I have been discussing, and one which is much more pertinent to a discussion of the civil list in connection with national defence. It is a matter I have already taken up with the minister, from whom I received a careful and sympathetic hearing. I am not speaking to-day to criticize the minister, but I am going to criticize some of the men-and I do not know what particular men they are,-for whom we are voting a part of this civil list. As I have said, I believe it is worth while to keep up national defence in Canada.
I can hold that view and at the same time I can reprobate what so often occurs-that a man because he is dressed in a uniform thinks he is justified in being an absolute autocrat in his attitude toward his fellow creatures. The man in the ranks has as good a right before this parliament as the officer at his desk, and I want to call the attention of this House, because there seems no other remedy for it, to a case of flagrant and prolonged injustice which has resulted in a young man being debarred from honest employment which ought to be open to him if he is telling the truth, and if he could get justice. It will not take very long-because I have made a memorandum of the case which I have already presented to the minister-to lay the facts before the House, and in that way before the country. I can get no other remedy but that of publicity, but this young man shall at least have that. His name is John Joseph Quilty, born on the west side of the harbour of St. John, New Brunswick. He was a railway employee with the Canadian Pacific Railway. At the time of conscription he was exempted on the ground of railway service. His serial number was 678783 E.C. The certificate stated that he was exempted until he ceased to be employed as a railway clerk. Now mistakes are not uncommon in any line of business, and Quilty in that certificate should not have been called a railway clerk. He never was one; he was a railway fireman. Nothing perhaps turns on this mistake except that it shows the possibility of innocent mistake, and unfortunately other mistakes occurred with regard to Quilty which he has never been able to get rectified. I have personally seen a document issued by local tribunal No. 35 in which Mr. Quilty is described by serial 678783 and consecutive number 528. It exempted him while in the railway employ. It is dated 21st December, 1917, and is signed by J. F. Owens and C. B. Lockhard. Both of these men and their signatures are well known to me, and there is no doubt of the genuineness of this document. Now up to that point Quilty was exempt.
Mr. Quilty tells me that a statement was posted in the Canadian Pacific railway yards Bayshore, West St. John, that these exemptions would continue, as there were limitations of time, I think, in nearly all the railway certificates which were issued'. He alone of all the men received a notification that he must appear and report for service. He did so, as he says, on 7th May, 1918, but the military record shows his enlistment on 6th May, 1918. He tells me that at that time no medical sheet had been received by the depot battalion. It appears from the records, that on the 15th May, 1918, the medical sheet was produced, showing that he had! been examined on 3rd October, 1917, and it also appears from the records, that he was examined by a medical board on May 6th, 1918. The earlier examination, of bourse, would be in connection with liability to service. His statement is that about four days after reporting he was told to sign some paper, which was probably an attestation sheet and that he was assigned to "A" Company. He claims that he was never issued any uniform and that while he occasionally reported, no

This brother was conscripted, went to the front, and made the supreme sacrifice. I am not aware that J. J. It is quite clear from the military records, that on 15th May, 1918, Qui'lty signed a recruit's declaration, as a draftee under the Military Service Act. On the same day he signed a form of will.
On the 12th of August, 1918, a court of inquiiy was held at Camp Sussex, some forty-four miles from the place to which Quilty had repared for enlistment. The court found that Quilty had illegally absented himself, without leave, on 15th May, 1918, the very day that he made his declaration and signed his will. One of the witnesses says that his kit was reported deficient, as stated in the evidence of C.Q.M.S. Hardy on the 17th day of May, 1918. It seems very strange that Hardy's testimony states that any articles were missing. It is evident that Quilty's statement that he was never issued a uniform is true, as the court's finding declares there was no deficiency, -another blunder in this evidence, not serious perhaps, and I do not wonder at mistakes occurring with the tremendous rush there was at those camps, but I do not want a blunder to blast a man's life.
No steps were ever taken to apprehend Quilty or to compel him to serve. On June 7, 1920, some two years after this occurrence, the Pension department of the Canadian Pacific Railway sent to the Militia department for inspection what purported to be a discharge certificate held by Quilty No. 326278.
On 16th June of the same year the Director of Records wrote to the District Record Officer sending this discharge certificate, which he states is thought to be a forgery. He pointed out-and this is an exact quotation from the correspondence on the subject-(1) That it

does not bear the headquarter's stamp; (2) That the form is obsolete; (3) That from comparison of the handwriting, it would appear that Quilty made out his own discharge; (4) That there is no record of any discharge in orders; (5) That the signature of Quilty on his regimental documents appears to be identical with his signature on the discharge certificate ; and (6) that there i3 no record of such a number as 326278. The District Record Officer replied to the Director of Records at headquarters on 28th of June, 1920, saying that from all appearances the discharge certificate is a forgery, as there is no record of same having been issued in that district. He attached a specimen of Major H. H. Smith's signature, Major Smith being the officer by whom the certificate purported to be signed. There is a photographic copy of the discharge certificate attached to the return of the papers in this case. It is signed by Quilty, as it should be. All the filled-in part is in writing, except the case of discharge, which is typewritten and is in these words "being no longer physically fit for war service K.R. & 0. 392 XVII." It is suggested, of course, that Quilty, who is a man of no great education, knew enough to turn up the King's Regulations and Orders and find this paragraph and put it in there as the proper thing-* an utter absurdity to any one who knows the young man. The description of age, height, complexion, eyes and trade, with a description of identifying marks, are all typewritten. The identifying marks are entered "nil." Now nil is a word that Quilty would never think of using. I am satisfied he would not understand it and the description does not correspond with Quilty's medical sheet.
Knowing the man as I do, it is simply incredible that he can have assigned to himself a number, which by the way was neither his regimental number nor that of his Military Service Act record; that he can have filled in part of the form with a typewriter, which I know he cannot use; that he can have filled in the remainder of it in a handwriting entirely different from his own, nor that he can have signed it in another handwriting. His handwriting is of a character-I could show hon. members copies of it-it is the handwriting of a man who can write only one hand. The signature on the discharge certificate certainly clearly resembles that of Major Smith, the district officer. If it is a forgery, I would say it is a mighty good one, and it differs very materially from the portion of the certificate which is filled in in handwriting. No one would accuse the same person of having filled it in and signed it, unless that person was a very competent forger.

Now I ask you to add to these things the difficulties a man in Quilty's position would have to encounter, a man not employed in a regimental office, in the way o: getting hold of the parchment form, as well as perhaps the greater difficulty of getting at the necessary records from which to fill in the material portions of the document. It is true he might have been in collusion with some man that could do these things. That is a possibility, but I do not think it is fair to assume this possibility against this man. The brass hats have done so. I want a trial by a jury of his countrymen, and not by brass hats. This certificate is dated 2nd May, 1919, nearly a year after he had enlisted. In other words he had been at camp Sussex where the decision of a court martial had rendered him liable to imprisonment and he is supposed to have forged, or obtained the forgery of, a certificate a year afterwards, as if that would do him any good. Not one of the considerations I have pointed out appears to have been present in the minds of the officers asked to report on this subject. The Adjutant General wrote to the Canadian Pacific Railway Pension department on 16th July, 1920, saying that the case had been thoroughly investigated by the District Record Officer of No. 7 district. He stated that the discharge certificate was a forgery and that-I quote his note- "the handwriting on this certificate is similar to that of the soldier, marginally noted (Quilty) who was struck off strength as a deserter at St. John on 15th May, 1918." If he means the signature it is similar, of course the man put his own signature on; he was directed to sign. If, however, he means the body of the certificate he could not have looked at the document because it is absurd to say that the handwriting on the signature, with the exception of Quilty's own signature, is similar to Quilty's handwriting. The most casual or the most careful inspection would-demonstrate the difference. He was advised that the discharge certificate, being a forgery, would be retained by the directorate.
Now, the action of the department-the casual, careless action of the department- resulted in Quilty's dismissal by the Canadian Pacific on the ground of his having been illegally absent from service, and the man who before the war was working in the employ of this railway was dismissed. He was no deserter, according to his story at all events; he was no shirker. He was exempted, under the law made by this parliament, which provided that the railway services of the country should be carried on by men just such as he. He gave up his discharge certificate, or 211
what he thought was his discharge certificate, so that it might be investigated. He has never up to this hour been able to get that document back; the department have impounded it and he cannot get it. I have seen in a return to this House a photographic copy of the certificate, but the man himself cannot get hold of it. While he has not been directly charged with forgery, it would have been far better, far fairer, and far more manly to have charged him with forgery. Then he could have got a fair trial by somebody who would not have had, at least, the prejudice of a military caste against the man. He is treated, however, as one in possession of a forged document apparently concocted for his own advantage. He is blacklisted by the railway, and has never had an opportunity to explain his conduct, his possession of the certificate, or to justify himself in any way. He has lost the advantages which, as a young man, he had in connection with an important branch of employment.
I personally brought this matter to the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) when he was Minister of Militia and Defence. He kindly instructed his department to report upon the subject, and in consequence the General Office^ commanding military district No. 7 stated on 10th February, 1921, that there were a number of men by tb; nar'e of McIntyre on the strength if the depot b&Qalion, New Brunswick regiment, and thai, it was *.-1 possible to trace the one concerned, in order to^erify Quilty's statement at so late a date. This man does not want a pardon; a pardon is only for a man who has been guilty of some offence. What he wants is an opportunity to vindicate his innocence.
I took the matter up again with the minister on 11th November, 1922, and on 5th April, 1923, received a letter from the minister in which he stated that he felt if the matter was fully explained to me I would appreciate that Quilty had no further cause for consideration by the department. The minister was of the opinion that it was logical to

Last year I laid this memorandum, practically as I have recited it to-day, fobfore the minister. I was assured of his sympathy, and I feel that I have it. I feel that he does not want any injustice done, but apparently he has not been able, as yet, to cut the official red tape. I am going to ask this House now to express its opinion that Mr. Quilty should be given his hearing before some civil tribunal,

so that if he is guilty of forgery he will stand convicted as a forger; but if he is not guilty the stain will be wiped from his character and he can re-enter the employ of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company honourably, as he claims he has a right to do.

The case to which my hon. friend has referred is typical of a great many other cases which arose in the department during the period of the war. One can well understand that during the years from 1914 to 1918, through the sudden responsibility that was thrown upon the officials of the department and the military officers of that time, a great many occurrences happened which, in the light of after events, appear to be injustices. There is not a week passes but there come to me from some part of the Dominion cases of men who claim that at various times they did not receive proper consideration from the officers having to do with them during the period in question. But the case my hon. friend has brought up is a unique one, and is out of line with the ordinary case of complaint which has been brought before me and before previous ministers. Certainly it would seem to be an anomaly that this young man should be in the position in which he is at present. I remember very well that my hon. friend called the matter to my attention some time ago, and it was rather difficult, even with the most sincere desire to meet his views, to indicate exactly what course could be taken by the department now in order to remedy the situation which arose as a result of previous actions which prevented him from being re-employed by the Canadian Pacific Railway. I say to my hon. friend that, realizing his evident sincerity in this matter, I shall be glad to take it up, and do anything in my power to relieve the situation in which Mr. Quilty is placed.

I suggest to the minister that he should get someone from the Department of Justice, or some competent legal man in St. John if he wishes, and give him authority under an order in council to investigate this matter. Let him see what information the department has, and let him hear the man himself. The point is that Quilty has never been before anybody yet to whom he could give an explanation of the circumstances. The district record officer from St. John would not send for Quilty, he looked over the document and gave five reasons why it was a forgery, and these reasons would not convince any man of legal

But they speak of the defence of Canada. Why, the pamphlet issued by the Navy League a short time ago stated that we might as well dismiss that idea from our minds, and that Canada was in no danger of attack; therefore -whatever preparations are to be made would not be for our defence. what we read, might mean the destruction of the human race in that part of the world. Is there any effort Canada could make that could change the course of events in such a. war? That point is well worthy of consideration. If there is anything Canada or the North American continent can do to preserve peace or promote peace, whether through the League of Nations, or a world court of justice, or in any way whatever, I believe every person in Canada would be glad by every means in his power to do it.
Is it just possible that Europe will destroy itself? Great empires and even civilizations have passed away, leaving scarcely a trace behind, and that part of the human race in Europe can destroy itself. Are they making preparations to do so? If these preparations go on, and if such a war should break out, could Great Britain save herself by withdrawing altogether from the continent? Could that part of the Caucasian race living in North America and South America save itself by withdrawing from Europe? There is no use in playing with matters of this kind. Any preparation that we could make within our power would hardly be a drop in the bucket compared with what would be necessary in order to take any appreciable part in any great war in Europe. I had a little experience myself when I was much younger than I am now. I was in the artillery service in a rural corps, and perhaps things are better now than they were then. I know the training we got in two weeks in the artillery, and I know the training the infantry got, and so far as the rural units are concerned, I have no hesitation in saying the whole thing was a farce, and the money was wasted. I would be prepared to admit that a city unit that could train in the drill halls in the winter season and keep up their training might get an education or a training that would be of service in case of an emergency; but I repeat again that unless things have changed very much, money expended in training rural units is money wasted, and I think we would be well advised to consider very carefully before voting large sums of money for any such purpose. These are the thoughts I wish to express, because the artillerymen for some reason or other- and it is not to their discredit-are nearly always anxious to make preparation for war. They think it is important; they think it will help to maintain peace. I believe they are mistaken; I believe it is the very means of bringing on war and of exciting peopie to the pitch of war. All the preparations that were made in Europe previous to the last war did not prevent war, and all the prepara-

tions they are making now for the next war will not obviate that one. A different mentality must be created if war is to be avoided and if that part of the Caucasian race that inhabits Europe is to continue to exist. The next war will mean the destruction of Europe and perhaps that part of the world will be peopled by the other races. It may be in the decrees of Providence that that part of the world shall be peopled by the Mongolian race, by the Asiatics. I do not intend
to discuss this or that particular item of expenditure but rather to consider the general principles underlying the policy of preparedness. I want to challenge the theory which underlies the whole of armaments, whether military, naval or air; that is, that armaments are in any sense a guarantee of safety. That is the underlying postulate of this theory. Now, some of us are interested in preserving the country but we cannot see that armaments are the means by which this can be done. As a matter of fact it would seem as if the last war had demonstrated to the whole world the futility of preparedness as a means of safety. Yet, even within this short time after the close of the last war the world seems to be threatened with a recrudescence of militarism. In the British Empire itself we find a changed policy with regard to Singapore which may bring on strained relations with the oriental nations. The minister himself has this afternoon suggested that he has information that would show that war in Europe is by no means improbable.

I did not
indicate that I had information to that effect at all. What I did say was that having visited Europe last year and having had an opportunity of attending the League of Nations and judging the mentality of Europe I was not by any means satisfied that the danger of war was over but that on the contrary war might take place.

I am glad to have the minister's statement in that regard. I think that, as undoubtedly anyone who has followed recent movements in Europe will admit, war in the near future is by no means improbable. We have Britain's own attitude towards Egypt and India, which is not at all reassuring to anyone who is outside the official circles. And we have recently had the Dawes

plan adopted. I am quite well aware that it was a Labour government that suggested the carrying out of a plan along this line. Nevertheless I believe that there is very real danger that the central part of Europe will be reduced to something resembling industrial serfdom. Undoubtedly the present political developments in both France and Germany would suggest that there is anything but the prospect of peace and security in central Europe to-day. Further than that, we have the anti-Japanese propaganda which is being carried forward in the United States and is being echoed in Canada.
Now, some hon. members may ask, what have we to do with Europe or Asia? Well, I venture to point out that we had a great deal to do with Europe when the last war came on, and there is no reason why we shall not have something to do with Europe again if other troubles arise.
The hon. member referred to Britain's attitude in Egypt and India. In order to get his point of view, he might tell us whether he would advocate the withdrawal of Great Britain from Egypt and India.

I do not know that I am called upon to answer that question; I made a general reference to Egypt and India, and I think that anyone who has followed to any extent the British policy in India during the past few years, with some of the types of repression which we have witnessed there, and with the refusal to give any large measure- of self government to India, must view the situation with anything but equanimity. And as we all know, Egypt has been a sore place for many years. We Britishers told the world that w^ were going there for temporary occupation, and so far we have neither withdrawn nor shown any signs that we are about to withdraw. However, I do not intend to discuss the policy of Great Britain in either Egypt or India; I .merely referred to the matter in passing. It might very well however be the subject of discussion in this parliament. Indeed, I had rather hoped that after we had set up a committee on international relations, we might discuss some of these questions in this House; because if the League of Nations is to mean anything to us-and through the League of Nations we are committed to certain definite responsibilities-and if the British Empire is to mean anything to us, especially in view of the fact that we are involved in war when the empire is involved in war, then we should have a little more discussion than we have had in past years of the policies that are carried on

by the British Empire as well as by other members of the League of Nations.
There are those who are perhaps inclined to deny any of us the right to question the maintenance of armaments. For a good many years in Canada those who believe in military preparation have had their innings, and they have almost come to take it for granted that their policy is the correct policy and the one that must be maintained indefinitely in this country. In fact, during the war it became a crime for anybody to question the causes that led to hostilities; and the press and other agencies effectually silenced anyone who was opposed to that policy. It seems to me that now that we have had this Great war, which has practically led to the bankruptcy of the world; and when we are faced with the possibility of another war, which as Winston Churchill has said will be the potential destroyer of the human race, it is well that we should take time to consider the claims of the militarists before passing as a matter of form from year to year these military estimates.
Some hon. gentlemen may say that this is merely a personal matter with me. I have no hesitation in saying that I was opposed to the last war, and I hope I shall be opposed to the next one. But it is not merely a personal matter. I was elected on a platform one plank of which advocated national disarmament, and I should not be true to the people who sent me here unless I took this opportunity to advocate that policy. Some hon. gentlemen here may pooh-pooh the idea ; but the fact is that a sufficient number of electors were found in the fairly respectable city of Winnipeg to endorse a policy of this kind. I have the right to stand here and voice the viewpoint of my electors. It is a viewpoint that is growing very rapidly across the country. I have in my hand a pamphlet which was issued just recently by a committee of the Protestant Ministerial Association of Montreal, in which strong ground is taken with regard to war and in which it is suggested, for example, that the Christian churches and Christian individuals ought in the presence of war to set God above Caesar, conscience above the. authority of the state. This, it seems to me, gives the state fair warning that if another war is precipitated, at least a section of the churches will refuse absolutely to participate in that war. Further than that, we have resolutions from farmers' organizations throughout the entire west protesting against the continued war expenditure.
As to the labour organizations, I think I cannot do better than read a paragraph or two from the manifesto issued about a year ago by the International Federation of Trade
Unions. This organization, let me interject, is not the one affiliated with Moscow. So there is no reason for any hon. gentleman to jump up and shout, "Red Moscow!" I note that the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada has signed this manifesto through its president, Tom Moore. The manifesto states:
We are drawing near the tenth anniversary of the day which saw the outbreak of the world war-that fatal August day which let loose Armageddon upon the world, and opened the way to a slaughter and havoo which has been unexampled in the annals of the world.
For four long years the world suffered untold agonies: for four long years the peoples fought each other like wild beasts; for four long years the flower of the world's youth was sacrificed on the battlefields: for four long years civilisation was forgotten, and its most elementary lessons were thrown to the winds.
During these four terrible years, thousands of young men went forth to battle in the confident hope that they were fighting to end war, and to make the world safe for democracy.
They did not know that they were merely the dupes of the lies and insinuations of small groups of capitalists, who were seeking to strengthen and extend their domination of the world.
Then came the sham peace that shattered the illusion of so many, and destroyed the dream that this was the war to end war.
And now the countries of the world are again making ready for fresh war.
Science is busy seeking new and even more terrible methods of dealing death and destruction. We all know that the next war will bring with it wholesale slaughter to a degree undreamed of before. The very air will he laden with death and will bring pestilence and destruction to countless multitudes far remote from the actual centres of war. The next war will be the final triump of barbarism; it will sweep from the face of the earth the last traces of civilisation.
In the next war there will be no place for personal heroism. The days when man could show prowess on the battle-field are for ever gone by. Henceforth he will be killed by a system of mass destruction, which will work unerringly as the machinery he now uses for mass production. The sole use of the mechanical perfection to which he will have attained will be to doom millions to horrible and inevitable death.
The manifesto calls upon the trade unionists throughout the world to unite in an international anti-war day. In view of this growing sentiment, I would suggest that we might very well pause and ask ourselves whether we should longer continue this policy, or whether we should give due notice to the advocates of militarism that we propose to insure the defence of our country along other lines.
Before following that theme any further, might I call the attention of the government to several specific matters? First of all, I notice very frequently by the papers that military officers-and in this connection the name of General MacBrien occurs very often- are taking the opportunity of going about the country advocating preparedness; in other words, devoting themselves to war propaganda. I would respectfully question

the propriety of salaried officials of the people of Canada undertaking to throw themselves into the advocacy of certain political policies. We do not permit it in other departments and I cannot see why it should be permitted in the National Defence department.
