Mr. Chairman, we have had definitely placed before us to-day the urgency of the situation and the need for preparedness. I submit with all respect that those of us who do not agree with that policy have a right to state our disagreement and the grounds on which it is based. '
As I was saying, we have constantly the glorification of our own nation, and side by side we have the habit of decrying other nations. One of the commonest ways of doing so is to call them nicknames. We have the Hun, the Dago, the Jap, the Chink, the Turk, and so on. All these names are derogatory in character, so that there is hardly a nation to-day but that if occasion should, arise, could be designated by some term of opprobrium. Thus it is easy to arouse great antagonism on the part of our people.
The fact is that even peace has been very largely an armed truce or simply a defensive alliance. Let me point out at the same time that we have recently experienced some very remarkable world developments. To-day we have an economic interdependence that has brought all the nations into close relationship the one with the other; I do not think I need to elaborate that statement. No nation today is self-contained. Each nation is inevitably connected with all other nations. It is

absolutely impossible for us, as it were, to put a corral around our own particular piece of property and say we will have nothing to do with outsiders. The whole of modern industry, commerce and finance is international, inter-communal in character. Thus there is a growing sense of world community. We have seen this for a great many years in the scientific world. We recognize that advancement in any one nation along scientific lines means advancement in other nations. We have seen it more or less in the cultural spheres, literary, artistic and religious. We know that what happens in any one part of the world is of more or less concern to all the rest of the world. But let me point out that with this growing inter-dependence, world-wide in its character, we have group and class conflicts that are also world-wide. The financiers do not stop within the bounds of one nation, but stretch their operations over into other nations. The present highly concentrated system of finance is also international in its viewpoint, and we have also our international labour unions, our international socialist parties, just as we have our international groups of financiers and industrialists.
The trouble, Mr. Chairman, is, I submit, that there is a danger of the various groups and classes using the political machinery and national prejudices for their own ends. It is so easy for the one group that happens to be for the time being in control to use the political machinery to advance business interests, and that has been done again and again; in fact, that is more or less the settled policy of the British Empire itself. We look back at the past war for a moment, and I think no one is any longer deceived as to its causes. President Wilson said at St. Louis:
Is there in this audience any man, or any woman, nay-is there any child, who does not know that the seeds of war are sown in hot, successful commercial and industrial rivalry?
Marshal Foch made a similar statement just after the war was over. Joseph Chamberlain years ago said:
The Empire is commerce	It was created
by commerce, it is founded on commerce, and it could not exist a day without commerce. . . . For these reasons, among others, I would never lose the hold which we now have over our great Indian dependency-by far the greatest and most valuable of all the customers we have or ever shall have in this country. For the same reasons I approve of the continued occupation of Egypt. . . . and lastly it is for the same reasons that I hold that our Navy should be strengthened, until its supremacy is so assured that we cannot be shaken in any of the possessions which we hold, or may hold hereafter.
A frank recognition that commerce is behind the whole of our military preparations to-day! A few days before the outbreak

Supply-Defence
of the Great war, Sir Edward Grey defined in the House of Commons on July 10, 1914, what had been for years the practice of the Foreign Office. He said:
I regard it as our duty, wherever bona-fide British capital is forthcoming in any part of the world, and is applying for concessions to which there are no valid political objections, that we should give it the utmost support we can, and endeavour to convince the foreign government concerned that it is to its interest as well as our own to give the concessions for railways and so forth to British firms, who carry them out at reasonable prices and in the best possible way.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I would submit to you that .this matter comes very close to us here in this House at the present time as we are considering these estimates. If we are inextricably involved with the British Empire and with the fate of the British Empire, and if it is definitely the policy of the British Empire to seek concessions in almost any part of the world, to develop certain markets in almost any part of the world, to extend its finance into almost any part of the world,-surely we are constantly in danger of being dragged into the various operations in which the British government is more or less concerned. Just before the last Great war Mr. H. N. Brailsford pictured in a very notable book, The War of Steel and Gold, the situation which existed at that time. It might have been called a prophecy of the war, because he showed how the whole stage was set for war, and that war was inevitable. I was surprised a little while ago to find the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) speaking as if there had not been preparedness on the part of England. If he will read anything of the literature which has come to us since the war he will find abundant evidence that there had been very, very definite preparations on the part of England as on the part of other nations, for the last great war. Mr. Brailsford in a recent issue of The New Leader, in commenting on British policy had this to say:
The foreign ministers of other great powers interpreted their "duty" in the same way-
That is, as Great Britain did,
-and felt the same touching confidence in the capitalists whose ambitions they promoted. The result was that, for a generation before the war, Constantinople, Pekin and. Teheran were centres of intrigue, in which the financiers and the diplomatists of all the great powers, in the closest association, cajoled and bribed and bullied, formed their cliques, hired their partisans, scrambled for loans and concessions, competed in selling armaments and railways and in buying oil wells and mines, and carried their competition from the field of business to the world of high politics. Should the "heavy industry" of Germany or of France dig iron-ore in Morocco in order to lay it down in the form of steel rails on the road to Bagdad?-that in one concrete illustration
was the question which set all Europe arming in two allied camps.
Sometimes the rivalry was checked in one region by an arrangement, fatal to the liberties of its population, to divide it into spheres of influence. Tropical Africa was in the end partitioned peacefully: Persia was amicably torn in two by Russia and Great Britain. But always the rivalry broke out again, for always and in every country the pressure of business and finance was at work in the press and among politicians to prompt governments to forge more cannon, to build greater battleships, to exhaust the last reserves of man-,power, in the effort to gain a preponderance of prestige and force which might be used for economic ends.
And. then Mr. Brailsford goes on to meet the objection that all this is a thing of the past, and that through the League of Nations we had created an instrument which was going to put an end to this kind of capitalistic manipulation. He proceeds:
"An old story," you may say, "an obsolete story. Capitalism has made the world safe for democracy and banished war by its League of Nations." Save by its attempts to regulate the hours of labour, the one thing which the league has not touched, or begun to touch, is this curse of economic imperialism. Under its shelter the predatory hunt for oil and coal, for raw materials to monopolise and territory to exploit, has been blessed and sanctified: it has not been stopped. We arm more heavily than before, and as before diplomacy places the services of the state at the disposal of capital invested abroad; while the British government insists that the league must not interfere between us and the population of our fields of investment in Egypt and the Soudan. Capital has acquired nationality: shares possess citizenship, and scrip can say in Palmerston's words, Civis Romanus sum. So long as private capital can call up, to guarantee its profits, the clerks of the foreign office and the admirals of the fleet, so long will it perpetuate militarism and prepare wars.
I have spoken, of the situation as it affects the British Empire. Now I should like to draw attention to the advocacy of preparedness that is being carried on in Canada. I hold in my hand a pamphlet issued by the Navy League of Canada in which we have a very excellent statement as to the real reason for armaments. It is entitled "The Interdependence of Canadian Industry and Naval Defence." I notice as patrons: His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, Their Excellencies Baron and Baroness Byng of Vimy; and the Lieutenant Governor of each province. I notice among the honourary presidents: E. W. Beatty and Sir Henry Worth Thornton. This document reminds me very strongly of another that I hold in my hand, dated August, 1912, when the same kind of propaganda was being carried forward. On this particular document Hon. D. C. Cameron, then Lietutenant Governor of Manitoba, headed the list. I also find the names of George Bury, Vice-president Canadian Pacific Railway; M. H. MacLeod, General Manager Canadian Northern Railway; Hugh Suther-
Supply-Dejence

land, Executive agent Canadian Northern Railway. So that it is the same class of men who now advocate preparedness as urged it before the last war. I should like to read two or three statements from the pamphlet in question which, I think, place the issue frankly and fairly. I am not throwing any discredit whatever on gentlemen who honestly believe this is the way to save our country; I give them every credit for their convictions in this regard, but I claim they should extend the same credit to us and admit that we are honestly endeavouring to put forward a policy which we on our part believe will save our country. This pamphlet puts the case so clearly that I wish to place it before the House:
That at the present time, and so far as can be forseen by the most idealistic statesmen responsible for the destiny of their respective countries, there :e no immediate prospect of certainty that the re-actions of various national external policies will not result in a call to arms to support antagonistic national convictions.
That to meet our obligations to future generations, the development of national industries must be on a basis of stability, and that stability is ephemeral under existing conditions, without the security provided by armed forces.
The question is asked on the next page:
What is a navy for? There is a common idea that the object of a navy is to resist invasion, and if that conception were correct there would be little to say in favour of naval defence for the Dominion. But it ia far from accurate, particularly as regards Canada.
The primary role of the navy is the protection of lines of communication across the sea. There are many ways in which the navy has to carry out this duty, many kinds of naval activities, but whether it be the clash of great battle-fleets, the cruiser actions, the submarine and mine blockade of enemy ports, the convoy escort work, the patrols of minesweepers and light craft off our coasts, or the many other distinct operations, they are each and all phases of the main objective of keeping the sea routes open and secure from enemy action.
The pamphlet in the latter part does what some of us have tried to get the minister to do on previous occasions, and does it very frankly It discusses the question as to who our enemies are likely to be. The view put forward is that there are three conditions of emergency or war in which we may become involved: First, our position as a neutral, with a very heavy responsibility, in the event of war between the United States and some overseas power; second, ourselves at war with an overseas power; and third, war with the United States. I do not propose to discuss whether, in any one of these three eventualities preparedness would be our best means of safety; I think that could very well be left to the House. But I read again, a statement of the underlying theory:

The fact is that the seeds, the root of war, ne
not in armaments but in economic causes, in the re-actions of varying national policies framed by governments with a view to the industrial and commercial development of their peoples. The economic struggle goes on to-day as actively as prior to August, 1914. Nations, with their varying economio problems, their natural racial pride, their own group psychology, evolve policies which it is vain to believe will all be in harmony, and which involves an ever present risk of a clash wherein stability of industrial commitments will lie only with those in a position to maintain their sea communications.
One more brief quotation. After the pamphlet has frankly admitted that the Washington conference changed the details but not the principles of national naval defence:
So we differ both from those who say that armaments prevent wars and those who preach that armaments are the cause of war. It is the everlasting economio war, which prevails in time of nominal peace, which has produced, and will produce, physical war.
There we have a -most important statement made very fairly and very definitely by the navy league. I agree with the navy league in this regard:
It is the everlasting economic war, which prevails in time of nominal peace, which has produced, and will produce, physical war.
So we have to conclude that the last war was not, as we were assured, the war to end war. It was, in fact, simply a skirmish. I think we have to go further than that,. and say that those who promised us that this was the war to end war are not men whose judgment can safely be followed; they have proved themselves blind leaders of the blind. They have led us into the ditch. I think the least that might be expected of them is, if not to confess how seriously they were mistaken, at any rate to give opportunity for the discussion of some other and some better way.
Why should Canada not strike out along new lines? The hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) had on the order paper a resolution, which, I am very sorry, was not reached, suggesting a peace bureau to foster and promote international goodwill and understanding. Why not? We are spending our millions upon war preparations, why not spend at least a few thousands in trying to find if there is not some other way? We have trodden the hard paths of war; why not explore the avenues that may lead to peace? You want the thing put on a business basis? Mr. Chairman, if Canada adopted an attitude of this kind and was foremost among the nations that definitely set themselves against war and assured her citizens that they would keep out of these great struggles, it would be the biggest advertisement that Canada could ever make before the nations of the world. Your Wemlbley exhibition

Supply-Interior
would not not be in it with the statement that would go forth that Canada was done with war. You would have no need further to spend your millions of dollars in inducing people to come to this country, because the people would be flocking from war-torn Europe, only too glad to come to a country where there was no prospect of war.
But let me not deceive the House into thinking that I believe that merely by setting up a bureau of peace we could solve the problem. I come back again to this clear-cut statement of the Navy League of Canada. "It is the everlasting economic war which prevails in times of nominal peace which has produced and will produce physical war." And I would urge that this House should devote some attention to studying the fundamental principles of our economic and social order. I know there are those who, as soon as one suggests that we should have some fundamental changes, shout "Socialism" and try to banish the thought. I am not afraid of the word "Socialism," which comes from a perfectly good Latin word which means comradeship, which means that to-day we as individuals are no longer living isolated lives; that no nation is any longer living an isolated, individualistic life, but rather that we are living in society in a thousand and one complicated relationships and that we must adapt our political ideals and our political institutions and our political policies to meet the new situation that confronts us. I am perfectly well aware that it is comparatively useless to appeal along these lines to many members of this House, but I would like to appeal beyond the walls of this parliament, to the men who at the front learned what war really meant, because I have found after conversations with them that the majority of them actually thought that they went out to fight in order to end war, to bring in democracy, to have a changed social order, and these disillusioned men are among those who will back up any effort to put things on a new basis.
In conclusion, I would like to appeal to the men and women who have dreamed of a better future for their children and for humanity, and who are willing to take some risks to make their dreams come true. I recognize that the policy which I have advocated would involve risks, but the present policy involves not only risk, but almost certainly a failure. Why not take those risks which are incident to the development of the new means of protecting our nation?
Item stands.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Argenteuil, Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Last year we
voted for salaries, $1,501,410.25 for the permanent staff at Ottawa, whose salaries are chargeable to civil government. The amount asked for this year represents a decrease of $63,867. Statutory increases in accordance with the Civil Service Act have been provided for and these total $21,305. The reorganization of some of the branches accounts for a further increase of $1,725 while three new positions account for $6,480. The decreases are effected by the abolition of twenty-six positions amounting to $49,390, while twenty-six positions not required1 amount to $31,020. There are twenty-six positions abolished, twenty-six positions not required, and one position is for six months only. These are the reductions. But there are three new positions and this makes the net decrease forty-nine.
Since last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes; these
are comparisons with last year's figures.

This is the first time
the estimates of the Department of the Interior have come up'. They should not be gone into to-night but I will not press the objection if the minister will undertake that they will be gone on with on one of the first three days of the week.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is intended that I should gtay only for a short while.

Not more than every
fifth word is audible down here.

I would suggest to the
hon. meihber that he come up here where he ought to be; there is plenty of room. The Department of the Interior, like every other department, should be gone into on a separate day on one of the first three days of the week; otherwise the motion to go into Supply is valueless as far as that department is concerned. However, so long as the minister undertakes that there will be a motion to go into Supply for his department on another day I shall be satisfied.

The right hon. gentleman
will remember doing the same thing.

Yes, but he gave an
undertaking.
Supply-Interior
Without any undertaking.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The objection is that we are taking up two departments on one day?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
anticipate getting through to-night. However, I am willing to give that undertaking, certainly; I have no desire to deprive anyone of any opportunity to ask questions.

Has there been any
merging of branches since last year? I understand that the year before the Irrigation branch was merged with the Water Powers.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No direct
heads of branches have been abolished but we have reduced our Land branch considerably. We have them all in the Norlite building under Mr. Greenway. Formerly they were under separate heads.
School lands with Dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: All land branches are under Mr. Greenway at the present time. The same men are in charge but they are under one control.
The minister reopened some sub-offices which had been closed before. Has he closed any sub-offices?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We reorganized a number of offices but I have not the list at hand. We gave Kamloops the status of a sub-office.
Have any sub-offices been closed?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There may have been one or two. I am not sure whether Yoho is still in operation or not. These are only one man offices which are kept on a commission basis in the outskirts where homesteading is going on.

I notice at the bottom of the estimates that there is reference to a saving by superannuation of $20,500. What does that mean? I have always thought that superannuation would involve the paying of two salaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is a departmental saving but the money comes out of the superannuation fund. There is a good deal of criticism with regard to the retiring of civil servants but under the Superannuation Act I do not think the government will pay

very much money. True, we did under the Calder Act, which called for a direct grant in many cases; but under the Superannuation Act, with 5 per cent levied on the civil servants, I cannot believe that there will be any heavy draft on the resources of the government.
The minister will understand what I mean; it mentions a saving.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is a departmental saving.
But their superannuation allowance goes on while other people take their places in the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not in this case, which is a saving to this department although it is not a saving so far as the general total is concerned. The superannuation must be paid out of the fund.

I do not see why it appears there. I notice it is not in any of the other departments, for instance, Indian Affairs or Insurance. I do not understand how there can be a saving through superannuation. The number of employees is given; those employees are paid; how would there be a saving of their salaries through superannuation?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Apparently
there were savings because certain employees were superannuated during the year. I understood the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) to contend that the mere superannuation of a civil servant was not a saving to the government. But it certainly is a saving to the department, providing the position is not filled.

It may be a saving to the department, but that saving will already be represented in the $1,462,000, which is paid to 768 civil servants. When you pay those employees, how can you save their salaries by superannuation? They are not superannuated, they are on the staff.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When retirements take place, for example, in the middle of the year, five or six months' salaiy is saved for that particular year.
For the year we are on now?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. We had
a saving of $20,500 last year. The estimate is $25,000 for this year.

How in the world can
that be? The department estimates that 768 employees will be required this year. If that many are required, and one of them is super-

Supply-Interior
animated in the middle of the year, there will be somebody to take his place.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. We think that by further reorganization we can cut down our staff, but the difficulty is to know just when it is in order to make the cut. We cut it by $20,500 last year. By adopting this course, if certain [positions become vacant some time during the year in a large staff like this, we estimate we can save this much money. Therefore we have cut the estimate to this extent. In other words, we have obligated ourselves to make the reductions as far as is practicable. I find in my experience that it is a pretty good thing to do this, because then the officials of the department keep within the estimate.
Has this ever been 'adopted before?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, it is
only done in this one department.

Do you provide for the salaries of a certain number of clerks for the year, and then in the early part or middle of the year, supposing one is superannuated, you save his salary for the balance of the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
That would be perfectly correct if his plaice is not filled.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It will not be filled because we have not the salary available for the position.

I would imagine there would be promotions, and possibly the junior position would be filled. Unless the minister can say definitely that for every superannuation there will be a reduction of one clerk, it would hardly be fair to take full credit for what would be saved by superannuation.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

Then I cannot see how you can possibly take credit for the full saving by superannuation. Supposing a man is superannuated, and his position is filled by the clerk immediately under him, and this 'promotion continues down to the junior. If on his promotion his position is not filled, then of course you subtract the salary formerly paid to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We set out last year to reduce our staff, and we think we can reduce it still further by co-ordinating the work and getting the employees into buildings where we can amalgamate the staffs. That is what we are trying to do. I cannot say at the moment, nor can the officers of the department, just when that particular position will be
abolished, because in effect that is what it means. That individual may go on the superannuation list, but the position itself will be abolished, and we will not require that salary for the balance of the year. This is more or less an estimate of what we will save in that way.

WThoever prepared this estimate and reached the conclusion that there was to be a saving of $25,000, must have had his mind fixed upon certain persons receiving certain salaries being superannuated at a certain definite period. The next thing that comes to my mind is, will those positions be filled? If so, and you are filling the junior position-the minister knows what I am referring to-when there cannot be that saying. But if the minister will tell the committee that the junior position will not be filled, then I at once concede that you would save the salary of the junior officer who is promoted and whose position is not filled. I think the best way to get at the explanation would be to turn to the page and consult the notes there which indicate how it is we are going to have a saving of $25,000. We would like to know the number of the employees, the salaries they are getting, and the dates upon which they will retire. Then we can figure up the saving for ourselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is just the difficulty; hence this is the method we have adpoted. We have a list of last year's positions, of which we abolished twenty-six, but I assure my hon. friend that at the time I could not have told him exactly hcfw it would work out. If we knew that we would only vote salaries up to the time the retirements would take place. Under our programme this year we estimate that we will abolish completely several positions and make a net saving of $25,000. Therefore we have taken that sum off our estimates.

I would not prolong the discussion for one minute, so far as I am concerned, if the minister said that this will be saved by the abolition of positions, because if they are abolished of course we do not pay the salaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the only way we can abolish them.
Is it based upon certain definite retirements, or is it a guess?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If we can
get certain amalgamations through within a reasonable time and get our staff coordinated we can put those savings into effect. At all events, we cannot spend more money than
Supply-Interior

we are asking for, so we are taking the responsibility of reducing the estimate to this extent.
That is done sometimes?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, I
favour this system very much. Sometimes we may not make the reductions in the direction we expected, but we have to make them before the end of the year in order to save the money. It is imperative in this case.
If you made it $125,000 it would be better.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think my right hon. friend will admit that forty-nine reductions constituted pretty good progress last year, and I am prepared to go on in that direction.

What mystifies me is
that this government shows reductions in all details, according to the professions of its ministers, but when you add the whole thing up it is the same as the year before.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is not in this case.
I say that in the individual cases it is less. This will all appear, though, in some other items.

Is the department endeavouring to make this reorganization, or is it being done by the Auditor General? When the new Auditor General was appointed we were told that his principal duty was to reorganize the civil service through the Audit Board. So far as we can ascertain he has not done anything in that direction of any consequence. His salary was placed at $15,000 because he was supposed to have some special qualifications for this work, but so far as I can see that phase of his duties has been entirely dropped and the departments themselves are attempting reorganization-in perhaps an inefficient way, if we consider the results that are being obtained. Will the minister explain the system that is being followed in this connection?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I can only
speak for my own department. One of the difficulties I found on coming to Ottawa was the location of the staffs in different places all over the city. The Lands branch, for instance, had its staff in three different buildings; now we have them all in one building, and that makes saving possible. With respect to the Auditor General, he has not appeared in our department up to the moment, although I should be glad if he would come in, because if someone not connected with any of 
the staffs would go into the matter some saving could perhaps be made. We have, however, been decreasing the numbers of our staffs year by year, and I think we are not losing anything in efficiency. There is an idea prevalent that the work that has to be done by the Department of the Interior must be decreasing. That is true to a certain extent with respect to surveys, but it does not apply to leases, details of homesteading, pre-emption sales and all the other ramifications of the department's activities. In respect to these branches I cannot see that very much reduction can be accomplished, but I am putting reductions into effect wherever they can reasonably be made.

What saving has been
effected in the Lands branch?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I shall be
glad to deal with that when we come to the vote providing for that branch.

On page
78 of the estimates of last year the total number of employees for 1924-25 is given as 816; this year the total number of employees for 1924-25 is given as 817. The total amount voted was given in 1924-25 as $1,500,737, whereas in the 1924-25 column of this year's estimates it is given as $1,501,410. Will the minister explain that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

Has the Civil Service Commission done anything to assist in the reorganization of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: All the reorganization is virtually in the hands of the Civil Service Commission. There is an officer of the commission in our department continuously, and he assists and makes recommendations to the commission, particularly with regard to any additions that are requested. The Civil Service Commission are not responsible for all the work, because we make the requests for the changes that are deemed necessary, and these are investigated and reported on by the officer to whom I refer. The recommendation of the Civil Service Commission must of course go with every move that is made.

Then I understand that in
this department the services of the Civil Service Commission have been utilized to effect what reorganization has been made?

Is provision made
in this estimate for the salary of the gentleman who was formerly Gold Commissioner of the Yukon, Mr. Mackenzie, who, according to the minister, has been brought to Ottawa to assist in framing a policy for administration in the Northwest Territories along lines which will protect the natives and conserve wild life?

speechtext: No; that is in the Northwest Territories vote.

After last
year's criticism, has the minister been responsible for undertaking any co-ordination of the survey work of the various departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We will
come to that under another item.
I am simply asking whether any attempt has been made to co-ordinate the surveys.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. I will deal with it when we come to it.
I notice there has been a reduction in this item of 863,868, and also in the number of employees. How many reductions are due to death, how many to superannuation and how many to dismissals?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Twenty-six positions have been completely abolished, and there are twenty-six more which up to the beginning of the fiscal year we were not sure would be required in the re-organization, but which we now know are not required; so we have fifty-two positions that are completely abolished. I cannot give my hon. friend details as to whether these men died or are retired, but there are fifty-two individuals whose positions have been abolished and we have created three new positions.

I appreciate that, because twice 26 are 52, and 49 from that leaves a difference of 3, but what I am trying to find out is this: If a position is abolished and the clerk who has been filling that position receives employment in some other department, then as far as the country is concerned there is no saving. We were given to understand that there was going to be some re-organization and economy effected as the result of the appointment of the new Auditor General and the Audit Board, and I thought perhaps there would be some in this department; may be there are; I wanted to 'find that out. I would like to ascertain from the minister whether, when a position is abolished in his department, the officer holding that position is dismissed or whether he
gets employment in some other department. If the latter is the case, and it applies in all the departments, the country makes no saving whatever as the result of these positions being abolished.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would have some difficulty giving my hon. friend details, but I do not think any of these 52 went to any other department. A nufaber of them have been retired, and we are constantly having resignations. I have no knowledge that any of these went into any other department. As a matter of fact, there was some controversy amongst the Civil Service Commission as to whether an individual who resigned or was retired or stepped out of one department was eligible for appointment in another department, and I do not think that has been entirely settled yet. I can say frankly so far as this department is concerned, that when the services of an individual are not required, if there is a vacancy in some other department, he certainly ought to be given the preference.
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But so far as I know, not one of these 52 has gone to any other department.
If I rightly understand, when any civil servant is dismissed, it is always as a result of an order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Then I would think the minister w'ould know. There would be some record kept when such a formality as an order in council is required to get rid of a civil servant, and it ought to be easy to keep track of the number who are dismissed. Can the minister tell me whether or not there have been any dismissals brought about by order in council so far as his department is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Do we
dismiss any individual?
I do not mean for misconduct, but because you wanted to abolish the office, or for any other good reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no recollection of that. Of course, every change in the department is recorded by order in council, and the majority of these cases would be retirements or superannuation. Then we have a number of young women who get married-

I would call that a promotion.
Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: And we have individuals who leave the service for better positions, but as regards these 52 I have no recollection of any of them having been dismissed. These are voluntary retirements or superannuations, and when they step out the positions are abolished.

I think the minister will appreciate what is in my mind, and if it is possible to get the information necessary, I would like to get it. If we want to find out to what extent the country has benefited by what is suggested, Ve must of necessity know whether these abolitions or retirements or dismissals put an end entirely to the employment of the individual, or whether he got employment in some other department. As I have already said, if the employee is simply transferred to another department, the country saves nothing by that whatsoever. The minister has been very fair. He tells me he does not recollect any dismissals or transfers. That is partly satisfactory, but I would think we could get this information without any difficulty whatever. because if a civil servant is dismissed for any reason an order in council is passed and a record is kept, and we ought to be able to find out how many dismissals there are and whether the employee ceases to be an employee of the government in any department.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I can
recollect only one being transferred in my department, and that was not this year; I do not recollect a single transfer this year. When the services of a man are required in some department, a transfer may be effected, but that seldom happens. I think I can assure my hon. friend that, these fifty-two are all out of the service entirely ncrw, but I will verify this for my hon. friend later, and be glad to answer his question fully.

That is the information I
want.

When a female employee
marries, does she automatically leave the service?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Not always.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
know of any in my department.

I believe we had a definite illustration of the consolidation of branches in the union of the Water Powers branch and the Reclamation Service. Can the minister give us the details of just what was saved in civil government expenses by the joining of these two branches, what

staff was dropped, and what new positions were created?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I can give
that information when we are dealing with Reclamation and Water Powers, which is a separate service from this. I will have a note made of the question.

I understand there
was a good deal of controversy last year over salaries, and that a revision of salaries was brought in this year, and that many complaints have been received in regard to that revision. Would the minister say whether that applies to his department, and if so, how are those complaints being dealt with?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This salary revision, as my hon. friend knows, has only been out about ten or twelve d'ays. It will be surprising if there are not complaints; there usually are, but so far none have reached me from the Department of the Interior, or indeed from any other department, and of course this department is affected just the same as any other.

Could the minister tell
the committee just what an economic adviser in this department is, and what services he performs?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The gentleman who filled that position was a Mr. Patton. As my hon. friend knows when the Conservation Commission was abolished the staff came to the Department of the Interior. Mr. James White, who has since retired, came for one, and Mr. Patton came with him. The latter was classified, I understand, under that head in the Conservation Commission, and performed in the Natural Resources Intelligence branch of our department the same service the next year. Mr. Patton is now, I believe, going to enter another branch of the service, the Finance branch. He will appear next year as a transfer; it will not be a reduction of the staff.
Not in the same capacity.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, in the same capacity.
What provision is being made to hear complaints of the civil servants in regard to salary revision?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is scarcely relevant.

The minister said, Mr Chairman, he anticipated complaints. As a matter of fact I have seen by the press, particularly the western press, that civil servants

Supply-Interior
are highly indignant at the salaries that have been fixed for them, they do not think they have been fairly treated at all. I presume those civil servants are entering complaints although, perhaps, the minister has not heard of any in his own department. The question I asked, Mr. Chairman, was what provision was being made, or has been made for the purpose of hearing and determining these complaints, if any?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend will understand the government has not the particular authority to hear complaints. The Civil Service Act makes the Civil Service Commission supreme in these matters subject to the action of parliament. The government cannot very well take action without the consent of parliament, because the Civil Service Act puts the control of the civil servants into the hands of the commission. Of course the government must take the responsibility of acquiescing in the adjustment of salaries by the commission; my hon. friend knows that the only remedy provided by the act, in case of a grievance, is a recommendation to parliament. All these difficulties are occurring in every department, and the grievances are being heard every day. Sometimes they are adjusted by the Civil Service Commission and sometimes adjustment is refused; cases of this kind are happening continually. With respect to the Post Office Department my hon. friend will remember that last year we offered to give a hearing to the executive of the employees after the adjustments were all completed; and I noticed the other day-
I only got this from the press, however-that the hon. the Postmaster General (Mr. Murphy) is having a meeting with the executive to discuss what they claim is a grievance so far as they are concerned. But under the act the only remedy for the government, if they wished to overrule a finding of the Civil Service Commission, would be to make a recommendation to parliament and have parliament pass on it.

Is there going to be
any special committee this year with regard to the civil service?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Well, the
promise referred to was made to the executive of the employees of the Post Office Department. My hon. friend will remember that during the controversy that was one of the features of the case. We asked the executive to delay any drastic action until the adjustments were all made, and then, if they still felt they had a grievance, we would listen to the recommendations which they might make.
That would be a com-mi.tee of the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
But there is no committee of the kind I referred to in existence at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

That is the question
I was asking, whether it was the intention of the government to have any committee of the kind this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot
answer that question.
Could the minister tell us why the Inemational Boundary Commissioner is dropped from the estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows Mr. McArthur is dead, and the duties he performed have been combined with those of the Director General of Surveys who now takes charge.

Would the minister explain to the House what is meant by "exploratory engineer?" I see there are some twelve or fifteen different kinds of engineers mentioned in these estimates, and I should like to understand what an "exploratory engineer" is?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Since the
abolition of the Conservation Commission we have had one or two engineers whose business it is to assist the municipalities in making a survey of their conditions. For example Mr. Kitto is one of the officers who perform this particular line of work. It is largely to supply them with industrial information, to give them advice if they ask it; it is only done upon request. For example this official was in Winnipeg a short time ago making a survey there for that purpose, and advising the city council on matters largely industrial. These officers came over from the Conservation Commission.
Is that work done at the expense of the city?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, it is
done at our expense.
T Tr. McQUARRIE:	May I ask how the
travelling expenses are dealt with? Is there a certain per diem allowance provided, or do the officers concerned put in claims for expenses at the end of their journey when they return to Ottawa? What restrictions or what supervision is there in regard to travelling expenses, to see that the amounts charged arc right and proper?
Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
With the
exception of a man who is going outside of Canada when by order in council his per diem allowance is fixed, he has to render a certified account for his expenses.

Is there any limit to
the expenses an official may incur? If he is travelling from here to Vancouver can he take a compartment, if he wishes, on a train, or is he limited in the matter of expenses? As I understand it in some of the provinces- I think, for example, in Alberta-they have found it advisable to put a curb on the travelling expenses of civil servants, and the employees themselves find it more satisfactory to have a per diem allowance; it costs the country less and the civil servants are better satisfied to have it that way. I think I mentioned this matter last year and the minister said he knew something about the system, that he was watching it, and that he would give it a trial, or something of that kind. I am told it worked out very satisfactorily in Alberta; and it has been suggested to me that the same system might be applied to the services of the Dominion, with a saving to the country and also, perhaps, with more satisfaction to the employees themselves. That is the point I am raising. Under the present system, as I understand it, a man goes off on a trip, comes back, puts in his bill for expenses and the bill is paid. There is practically no restriction as to what expenses he may incur as long as they are considered to be in reason. There is no attempt at economy whatever. Apparently the government is satisfied to allow things to go along in the same old way, making no effort toward economy. Could the minister tell me if this point has ever been considered by this government, and if so what conclusion has been arrived at and what were the reasons for such conclusion?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Usually most people would prefer to travel on a per diem allowance, because that per diem allowance must be sufficiently large to cover their expenses. They get an allowance sufficient to provide for reasonable accommodation, and we have a very close check upon these accounts, which are checked by our own auditors and our own accountants, in our own department, and rechecked by the auditor. As I am a member of the Treasury Board, I know pretty well that there is not very much leeway. In addition to that, these accounts must be certified. If I were to give my candid opinion I would say that we save money by asking for the return of the vouchers for the accounts and by the careful checking that goes on. I will mention 
one instance. We have a good many removals, running into a considerable sum of money. These come before the Treasury Board and we have any number of them on every occasion on which the Treasury Board meets. We find that by careful checking we have been able to cut the removal expenses very considerably. I am not taking any credit, but I want to point out to hon. gentlemen that these accounts are scrutinized, because there is of necessity a great deal of travelling in the service, for that reason we have a careful check on all the accounts for travelling expenses.
Does this item of $32,000 include all the traveling expenses in the department for the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Then we have travelling expenses and sundries. How much is for travelling expenses and how much is for sundries?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is estimated that a sum of $22,000 will be required to meet the expenses of officials at Ottawa, permanent or temporary, who may be travelling on government business, and an amount of $10,000 will be necessary to cover the expenses such as telegrams, postage, subscriptions to newspapers, express charges, and other items relating to the inside service of the department at Ottawa.

Then does the item
above that, printing and stationery, relate to printing and stationery outside of the Printing Bureau?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Printing Bureau charge us for that work. Nothing goes outside.
Nothing at all goes outside?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, that is for index books for the Registration branch, land patent record books, special paper for patent printed form, purchase of typewriters and supplies and stationery required for the general use of the inside service at Ottawa.

There is no outside
printing at all in this particular branch of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
No advertising or anything of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No.

Supply-Interior

The .minister spoke of employees being transferred from the Conservation Commission to his department. Could he tell us how many of the 817 employees were transferred from the Conservation Commission, how many lare left now, and how
9 p.m. long before they will be out of the service? This service I understand has been done away with and the Conservation Commission abolished practically.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, that
is not correct. Part of the service is being continued in the Natural Resources Intelligence branch of the service, but these employees were in the department when I came here.
I cannot tell when they were transferred.

How many of the 817
were from the Conservation Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot
tell how many came over, it was before my time and we have not a record of the names.. It would be very difficult for me to tell, except as to two, Mr. White and Mr. Patton. Mr. Patton is still with us and will be exchanged; Mr. White is retired. I cannot tell my hon. friend how many of that particular group are still in the service.

I do not wish to delay the item, but this seems a good opportunity to ask for something in which I feel a little interested and possibly the matter may be dealt with in some publication. If so I want to see it. I am not objecting to what we are spending for this astronomical research work, but I would like to know the results we are getting from it. Have any discoveries been made or any works carried out that are of practical benefit? I do not mean to criticize if they are of practical benefit, but at the same time I would like to know what the relation is between what we get and the money we spend.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid you have given me a rather difficult question to answer. As a layman I frankly confess that I have not any doubt that the service is a valuable one to the country, but as a layman I would have considerable difficulty in explaining the value to my hon. friend. We spend a good deal of money on the service and no doubt the investigations are valuable, but just to put it in a concrete way, would be very difficult. However, when the vote comes up I will get that information.

I see provision made
here for four editors, grade 1, at $2,400 per annum or a total of $9,600. What are their duties?
212i	i '

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We get out a Natural Resources Intelligence Monthly to advertise the natural resources of the country, new discoveries of mineral wealth, and so forth. Our reports must be put in the hands of someone competent to take care of them and he is called editor. I do not want to be responsible for all these titles; I am merely stating the duties they perform.

There are also two
publicity agents. What are their duties?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have
Mr. Campbell now at Wembley. The business of these men is to advertise the scenic beauties of Canada, to encourage the tourist traffic. That is all they do.

I suppose the minister
knows that the Canadian National Railways have a bureau which is doing the same thing. Do they work in co-ordination with these publicity agents of his department or do they work on their own hook?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific both maintain services of this kind, and although the Canadian National Railways belong to the country, Mr. Campbell does not advertise them particularly; he is trying to induce people to come to Canada rather than to go to Europe to spend their wealth while travelling. We are bombarded by boards of trade all over the country to assist them in advertising campaigns and I think the time has nearly come in Canada, in view of the increasing importance of the tourist business here and the large amount of money it is bringing into the country, when there should be some co-ordination throughout the Dominion. For example, I think the city of Vancouver spends thousands annually in advertising. I am not complaining about that of course, but I cannot help feeling that great, good would result from such co-ordination as-exists in connection with fire fighting and better methods of forest conservation and preservation. Something of this kind in relation to the tourist business would help materially.

I am inclined to agree with the minister. I realize the value of the tourist business of this country and I am not criticizing in the slightest degree the expenditure under this head. There is no doubt that tourists along the Atlantic and in the mountains leave millions of dollars here which otherwise would not come to Canada. In New Brunswick we have a provincial tourist
Supply-Interior

association and the city from which I come maintains a tourist bureau. The same is true of all the principal centres in the Maritime provinces. I think it would be an excellent idea to have some co-ordinated effort to prevent the enormous over-lapping that now exists.

In line with the minister's
remarks os to co-ordination in tourist advertising for the purpose of inducing tourists to come to Canada, the publicity bureau at Vancouver in charge of Mr. Davidson submitted such a proposal to the government. Other tourist organizations in the various cities throughout the country are also interested in this matter; and the suggestion is that the government, in formulating a policy in this direction, as well as contributing to its upkeep, should aim at an advertising campaign that would be nation-wide rather than sectional. The idea should be for example that the bureaus of Ontario while participating in a nation wide policy would also try to induce tourists in the United States adjacent to Ontario to come to that province, and similarly the people of British Columbia would endeavour to bring tourists to British Columbia. I might tell the minister that, contrary to his idea, the city of Vancouver is not working in isolation; it has established a practical policy of co-ordination, having joined with the states of Oregon and Washington, under what was known as the Pacific Northwest Tourists' Association, in an extensive advertising campaign through the medium of hotels and otherwise to induce thousands of citizens to come from California and the middle states up to Portland, Seattle, .and Vancouver. British Columbia and the two .American states are treated as one territory :'for this purpose. I think the minister might profitably inquire into the results of this practical scheme. If he does he will find that it has been eminently satisfactory and has *brought into British Columbia many thousands of tourists who otherwise would never have gone there. Did the minister not receive a proposal of this kind some time ago, and in view of his remarks would he not be disposed to take the initiative in bringing together the advertising bureaus of the cities of Canada and other interested organizations to carry out such a policy as he has suggested to-night?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have
memoranda from Mr. Davidson on the subject and I had the pleasure of a visit from him last year and this year as well. We are preparing to put on what will be more or less a week of broadcasting for the pur-
pose of getting tourists to come to Canada right across the country. Our difficulty is that we must be extremely careful about our advertising, and that is why co-ordination appeals to me. I say frankly that so far we have done very little advertising in the way of newspaper or pamphlet publicity in the United States. We have contented ourselves with sending lecturers throughout the country at important points where large gatherings could be got together. These people have lectured on the scenic beauties of Canada, not emphasizing any particular part of the country; and the intensive local work has been carried on by organizations such as that maintained at Vancouver. The results have been splendid. I am quite prepared to take the initiative in getting together all the forces to see whether we cannot co-ordinate the efforts of the railways, the municipalities and the government in a drive to secure tourists. There may not be over-lapping at the moment but there is a possibility of some duplication with all the separate units working independently.

I have had occasion to
go into this matter in detail, having been connected in a professional way with a very large organization, the Brewster Transport Company at Banff, as well as with the Terminal City Motor Company and Triangle Tours at Vancouver. I am also acquainted with the activities of other organizations. I know that those men connected with the tourist business who have made a great success advertise the tourist features in a scientific way. This method does not appear to be followed by the government agencies. Experts in the tourist business do not give lectures. They ascertain when any organization is making arrangements for a convention, they send representatives to the chairman of the committee which has to do with selecting the convention city, and these representatives are provided with a plentiful supply of maps, photographs and other information, which they lay before the chairman of the committee. In a word, they are expert salesmen of our natural beauties, and they are very successful in bringing conventions to our cities. As a result of their efforts the tourist traffic across Canada in prospect next year, from information I have gathered, which has been confirmed by our railway executives, is simply tremendous. For instance, in one day alone 2,200 people will visit Banff and Lake Louise. These tourist organizations co-operate with the railways in securing this business. My suggestion is that the publicity bureau at

Supply-Interior
Vancouver and other cities be called upon to co-operate with the railway organizations which desire to get business for their railways! I would urge upon the minister the wisdom of the government taking the initiative in this work and not continuing its policy of drifting, because the tourist traffic means millions of dollars every year to Canada and to British Columbia. No doubt the minister has the data in his files, and if he studies it he will be surprised at the amazing advantages which are derived from practically no capital investment through inducing hundreds of thousands of people to visit the Dominion every year, for they leave a large amount of money behind them and spread a knowledge of Canada throughout other lands.

It seems to me that the government should adopt some general policy rather than a local one which might benefit only certain portions of the Dominion. Does the hon. gentleman suggest that the government deal with it locally?

I was simply suggesting
that the government should call together the people who understand the business of inducing tourists to visit our cities; in other words, that it should take the initiative and encourage those engaged in the business by intimating that the government will participate with them financially in working out a policy that would be of national advantage.

Is any publicity carried
on for the province of Quebec, and especially for the county which I have the honour to represent in this House, a county in which is situated the great summer resort of Murray Bay? Also, is any of this publicity work carried on in both languages, and particularly in the French language?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The government advertises the whole Dominion without specifying any particular locality.
That is a mistake.

Perhaps the minister
would inform us if these publicity agents organize the parties of tourists which from time to time visit this country from the United Kingdom. Three large parties of teachers from the United Kingdom will visit Canada this year. Hitherto' such parties always begin their tour at Quebec and proceed westward. Now, we do not wish to convey to these teachers a wrong geographical impression of this country, and it would be rather unfortunate if they imagined for one moment that the Dominion begins in the east in the city and
province of Quebec. I would suggest to the minister that whether his publicity agents organize these parties or not, he should send them a true map of Canada, so that intending tourists may obtain a correct geographical idea of the Dominion, and thus begin their lour further east than Quebec before proceeding westward through that province and the other fine portions of the Dominion. I am satisfied thait his publicity agents need this point drawn to their attention. I do not say that this ignoring of the Maritimes is deliberate, rather it is a habit with these people, and there are many instances of it in o:her departments, but I think the minister can help the situation materially by taking action along the lines I have suggested.
What system of distribution is adopted with respect to the publications which are got out by the four editors?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have a mailing list and are glad to send the publications to anybody who applies for them. This list is steadily growing. My hon. friend will notice that many of the articles in the Natural Resources Intelligence Monthly are quoted very largely by the press throughout Canada. A notable instance is Toronto Saturday Night, which my hon. friend will agree is a very important journal.
Have you some system in making up the mailing list, or is the work done in a blind way that does not really accomplish anything?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If, for example, an individual asks for a copy of the Natural Resources Intelligence Monthly, we put him on the mailing list. We treat him in a sense as an interested party.

You do not send the
publications to people who do not happen to ask for them?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We do not.

I understand that the
minister does not use the newspapers or the magazines for advertising purposes; he relies on his lecturers, of whom he has two, and on these publications, which -are sent out by his department to people who ask for them. Has he ever considered the question of a more extensive distribution of -these publications, some of which contain very valuable material?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In former
years these publications were sent out indiscriminately and mar" ~f -them were seldom
Supply-Interior

if ever read. Now we send them out to those who are interested in them. The circle of distribution is constantly enlarging, and we know that those we do send out are read and appreciated.

I agree that indiscriminate distribution would not produce results, but to distribute only to those who request them is not enough. The object, I take it, is to interest people in Canada, people who perhaps are not thinking about Canada at all. You will never get them with this system, or this lack of system. Are these publications distributed outside of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes-to the United States, for instance, to England, to the continent.
Are they printed in both French and English?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.
iMr. BOYS: How many are on the mailing list at present?
Mr, STEWART (Argenteuil): I have not that information before me but I will get it.
I notice that there are three senior jfhotographers and three photographers. What do they do?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They do
work connected with the aerial surveys, natural resources and intelligence, and the observatory.

I notice that all these departments have a departmental solicitor, and at the same time we have an expensive Department of Justice in which there are half a dozen good lawj'ers. Is it really necessary for every department to have ia lawyer of its own?

speechtext: In our department we need a great deal of legal advice. The schedule is the important part if there is anything important in the bill. Now we come to the expression "foreign country". Article 1 reads as follows:
Articles the produce or manufacture of Canada imported into the Netherlands and articles the produce or manufacture of the Netherlands imported into Canada shall not be subjected to other or higher duties or charges than those paid on the like articles the produce or manufacture of any other foreign country.
Now, the question I put before is pertinent. Unless that is modified in the remaining part of the article it would mean that the Netherlands could give to the other parts of the British Empire treatment better than to us. I read further:
Nor shall any prohibition or restriction be maintained or imposed on the importation of any article the produce or manufacture of Canada into the Netherlands, or of any articles the produce or manufacture of the Netherlands into Canada which shall not equally extend to the importation of like articles being the produce or manufacture of any other foreign country. [Mr. Meighen.l

it is a matter of what the words "foreign country" mean:
Articles the produce or manufacture of Canada imported into the Netherlands and articles the produce or manufacture of the Netherlands imported into Canada shall not be subjected to other or higher duties or charges than those paid on the like articles the produce or manufacture of any other foreign country.
Now then-

Any British country is a
