I would take it that the wording would allow us to give Great Britain,
or any of the British colonies a preference over the Netherlands.
I do not doubt that.

But I do not take it
that the article would allow the Netherlands to give Great Britain or any of the British colonies a preference over Canada, because Great Britain, or any of the British colonies, is a foreign country to the Netherlands the same as we are; while neither Great Britain nor any of the British colonies is a foreign country to us. I think the article preserves the right of Canada to give Great Britain or any of the British colonies a preference over the Netherlands; but it would preclude the Netherlands from giving either Great Britain or any of the British colonies a preference over Canada. That is my view of it, although I may be wrong.

Canada-Netherlands Convention

Does not the minister contend that "foreign country" as used in article 1 means every country other than Canada? Because this is an agreement between the Netherlands and Canada, and as the minister has said Great Britain is a foreign country to the Netherlands; and if it applies as a foreign country to the Netherlands, one of the parties to the treaty, it surely must apply as a foreign country to the other party to the treaty, unless there is a reservation.

My right hon. friend and the
chief whip of the Conservative party are good lawyers. Well, I will read it this way to see if it is not quite clear:
Articles the produce or manufacture of Canada imported into the Netherlands shall not be subjected to other or higher duties or charges than those paid on the like articles the produce or manufacture of any other foreign country.

I quite agree with the minister there. The difficulty is, this is an agreement between two countries, and you cannot put an interpretation upon certain words in that agreement which interpretation will mean one thing when applied to one of the parties and a totally different thing when applied to another of the parties;	and
"foreign country" as used there it does seem to me applies to every country other than Canada in the one case and other than the Netherlands in the other. Therefore, in that sense, Great Britain would be a foreign country to Canada for the purposes of this article. If the minister reads it I think he is bound to come to that conclusion.
Not at all.

Let me see if I cannot make
the point clear. The minister admits that Great Britain is a foreign country so far as the Netherlands is concerned. I think that is admitted, I think the minister has said that.
Yes.

Well then, let us again state
that this is an agreement as between two parties. If this foreign country means Great Britain, so far as the Netherlands is concerned, how can it mean anything else in the same agreement between the same two parties when applied to Canada? And if the intention is that it should, there should be some reservation.

The article appears quite clear to me. In the first place it says:
Articles the produce or manufacture of Canada imported into the Netherlands shall not be subjected to other or higher duties or charges than those paid on the like articles, the produce or manufacture of any other foreign country.
Read it the other way.

Reading it the other way:
Articles the produce or manufacture of the Netherlands imported into Canada shall not be subjected to other or higher duties or charges than those paid on the like articles the produce or manufacture of any other foreign country.
Foreign country would include Great Britain.
No.

That is the difficulty the minister is in. I think if he will look at other treaties of the same kind he will find an express reservation which apparently has been neglected here. If the words "foreign country" were used in relation to ourselves alone, the minister would be right, but he cannot say to the Netherlands, "Those words mean one thing to us, but they mean another thing to you," and without an express reservation the minister has got himself bound to either one of two things.
No.

Either he has to give
the Netherlands the same treatment as he gives Great Britain, or the Netherlands will be free to give Great Britain better treatment, the same as we are free to give Great Britain better treatment-one or the other.

No. My recollection is that
this was referred to the Justice department, and if my hon. friend has any doubt as to the definition of it, I am prepared to let the measure stand and again refer it to the Justice, department, but my own mind is quite clear.

It is not so much a doubt as to the definition, it is as to the application. What I cannot understand is how the minister can think that when these two countries are parties to the agreement, and in the body of that agreement the words "foreign country" are used, that in the one instance "foreign country" as applied to the Netherlands would refer to Great Britain, but although used in the same agreement, applying also to Canada, with no distinction, with no re-10 p.m. servation, he would put a totally different interpretation on the words as applying to Canada.

The effect of the treaty is that it is understood that in all matters governing the import, export and transit of merchandise the Netherlands grants to Canada, and Canada grants to the Netherlands the treatment of the most favoured nations. What does the wTord "nation" mean there? It does not simplify matters and does not

Canada-Netherlands Convention
solve the difficulty at all to tell us it has been before the Justice department. The department has no standing such as that of a tribunal which can deliver a judgment and force people to accept it. The Department of Justice merely expresses an opinion and it may be correct or it may be incorrect. But the opinions expressed in this House are quite on a par with those expressed by the Department of Justice.

In one point of view, England is not a foreign country to Canada; but at the same time, by reason of the fact that this language is used in the one sentence without even a comma, I think it might be advisable for the minister to let it stand and consult the Justice department, in view of the discussion which has taken place to-night, and make sure of the point, because it might be a serious matter if this interpretation should be as the leader of the opposition seems to think it is. Personally, I do not agree with him but I am not a lawyer and I do not want to pass a legal opinion on it, but I think the minister might be well advised to let it stand.
The minister negotiated this treaty himself, did he not? Did he make it clear to the Dutch negotiators?
Quite.

It is certainly doubtful enough to warrant a confirmation. I would not like to hold up the treaty, although it is not a very important one, but I would suggest that the minister confirm that interpretation by cable, and that would be far more important than the opinion of the Department of Justice or the opinion of anyone. Being a treaty between nations, it is not really a legal point. It is just a question of what a reasonable man reading it would likely take out of it. I fancy too that two out of three would say that what is a foreign country to one is a foreign country to the other in the same treaty, and the minister would be very well advised to get the interpretation he puts on it confirmed by the government of the Netherlands by cable, because it would be extremely serious if we bound ourselves, without any concession, to give to Holland and the Dutch colonies the British preference right off or any other preference we ever give Great Britain.

I would not like to go so far to say that we are going to re-open this with the Netherlands, but on Thursday when the matter was before the House objection was

taken to this bill on the ground that it did not clearly define whether or not the goods should come in through Canadian ports, and I promised then to refer it to the Justice
department. I have here the report of the Justice department, and reading it over, it makes it pretty clear. The report reads:
Department of Justice,
Canada.
Ottawa, 16th May, 1925.
Re: Convention of Commerce between Canada and the Netherlands
Dear Sir:
Referring to my interview with Mr. Russell and Mr. Viets of your department, regarding the question which arose in a discussion in the House, reported at pages 3181 and 3182 of Hansard of the 14th May, 1925, I beg to advise you as follows:
By Article XIV of the Convention of Commerce between Canada and France, 1922, it is provided that:
"To enjoy the benefit of the tariff advantages provided for in the foregoing articles products originating in and coming from France, the French colonies, possessions and protectorates shall be conveyed without transhipment from a port of those territories or from a port of a country enjoying the benefit of the preferential or intermediate tariff into a sea or river port of Canada.
Reciprocally to enjoy the benefit of the tariff advantages provided for in the foregoing articles the products originating in and coming from Canada imported into France, the French colonies, possessions and protectorates shall be conveyed direct from a Canadian port without transhipment in any country that does not enjoy the said tariff advantages.
Provided, however, that nothing in this article shall exempt the product of either country from any sur-taxe d'entrepot that is now or hereafter may be imposed on products imported indirectly."
In the subsequent convention made with Italy in 1923, and in the present convention with the Netherlands, no similar clause is to be found, but it is provided by Article I of both conventions as follows:
"Articles the produce of manufacture of Canada imported into the Netherlands and articles the produce of manufacture of the Netherlands imported into Canada shall not be subjected to other or higher duties or charges than those paid on the like articles the produce or manufacture of any other foreign country. Nor shall any prohibition or restriction be maintained or imposed on the importation of any article the produce or manufacture of Canada into the Netherlands, or of any articles the produce or manufacture of the Netherlands into Canada which shall not equally extend to the importation of like articles being the produce or manufacture of any other foreign country. This last provision is not applicable to the sanitary and other prohibitions occasioned by the necessity of protecting the safety of persons or of cattle, or of plants useful to agriculture."
As I interpret this provision, it clearly means on the one hand that articles the produce or manufacture of the respective countries shall not be subjected to other or higher duties or charges than those paid on the like articles the produce or manufacture of any other foreign country, and that on the other hand either country is free to impose any prohibition or restriction on the importation of such articles if such prohibition or restriction equally extends to the importation of like articles being the produce or manufacture of any other foreign country. Having in view these provisions, and the fact that both countries understand that the purpose of the convention is to extend to each other what is known as most favoured nation treatment, I see no

Canada-Netherlands Convention
reason to doubt that Canada has the right to impose the same prohibitions or restrictions under the present convention as were imposed in the convention with France above referred to, and which are in fact imposed with respect to all foreign countries enjoying most favoured nation treatment. If, therefore, appropriate legislative sanction exists for the imposition of any such prohibition or restriction, I think that no difficulty with the Netherlands will arise. Inasmuch as the provisions of article I of the convention above quoted clearly indicate that the intention of the convention was to permit the imposition of prohibitions and restrictions of the kind mentioned, I think that _ if clause 4 of the bill approving the convention be enacted as drawn, it will constitute sufficient legislative sanction for the making by the Governor in Council of such orders and regulations as are deemed necessary to put such prohibitions or restrictions into effect. I understand that a similar clause was incorporated in the bill relating to the convention between Canada and Italy, 1923, and I would not, therefore, vary the wording of the clause if it can be avoided.
The above remarks apply as well to the convention with Finland.
Yours truly,
W. Stuart Edwards,
I think that makes it pretty clear that we are safeguarded.

I am not taking exception to the deputy minister's opinion but I want to point out to the minister that in his resolution as he introduced it there was not included a full statement of article 1 and of the reservation contained in the second sentence here:
Nor shall any prohibition or restriction be maintained or imposed on the importation of any article the produce or manufacture of Canada into the Netherlands, or of any articles the produce or manufacture of the Netherlands into Canada which shall not equally extend to the importation of dike articles being the produce or manufacture of any other foreign country.
That is the restriction on which the deputy minister relies and, I fancy, relies correctly. What the minister said before was that merely because it was in the French treaty we could therefore apply it to the Netherlands. But it would not apply at all. It is in the French treaty, and the only importance it has is this, that if it were not in the French treaty we could not apply it here, notwithstanding this second sentence. But because the second sentence appears, then, it being in the French treaty, we can apply it to the Netherlands. If the minister had the second sentence in his resolution there would be no question at all in the House and he would not have had to go to the Justice department. This is a matter where Holland is bound to consider Great Britain, in relation to trade matters, a foreign country as respects Canada. If I were in a court I would rather have Holland's end of the case. In so far as Canada is concerned, in her trade matters one country is as foreign
to her as another. Holland could very well say to us, "We are dealing with you alone in matters of trade, and if you are going to give a preference to one nation you must give it to us. We are not concerned with your internal relations."

The minister will remember that in recent years it has not been infrequent in certain quarters to emphasize the fact that Canada is a nation. I am not finding any fault with that; but having laid the fact down in such emphatic terms, when we read the word "nation" in a convention of this character it must surely have the meaning we have been attaching to it; and if Canada is a nation Australia i3 equally a nation. Is it really the opinion of the government that they cannot deal with Australia for instance, as a component part of the empire and yet a distinct entity within the empire, on a better footing than they can deal with the Netherlands? Or is it the deliberate intention of the government to .so bind us that whatever concessions we make to Australia must, automatically operate to the benefit of the Netherlands? If that is what the minister intends to do he has in my judgment succeeded in doing it by article 4 of the treaty. If that is the intention of the government and they take the responsibility of it there is nothing more to be said; they are in charge at the helm and this is the direction in which they wish to steer. But if the minister does not intend to do that I can say to him with the most positive assurance that the language employed is not effecting his purpose but a very different one. Like my right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen) I . would advise him, if he does not mean to do this, to hold the matter over until he has made the thing perfectly clear in a diplomatic way; otherwise the result I have indicated must absolutely follow.

I cannot allow my hon. friend to put into my mouth or to ascribe to the government ideas which were never entertained. My hon. friend is a good lawyer and he might plead a case well before a court of law, but I do not intend to get into any argument with legal gentlemen regarding the phraseology of this bill. I am satisfied that the bill declares exactly what was intended, that we should give the Netherlands our intermediate column of tariff, or a little better m some cases, wherever we have conceded it. But there is no intention of giving them the British preference, and I am satisfied that no court would hold that. However, if it will satisfy my right hon. friend I will undertake,

This gradually moving into the guarantee atmosphere-no guarantee one year; a moderate guarantee the next year; a far bigger one the next year, and the cash advances growing in the reverse order-well, it just gets the whole country confused and gives politicians who must confuse, to avoid calamity, an excellent opportunity to do so.

The House in committee on Bill No. 74, respecting the construction of a line of railway forming part of the Canadian National Railways between Bengough and a point at or near Willowbunch, in the province of Saskatchewan, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-power to construct and complete line described in schedule.

I would like to
get an understanding with my hon. friend as to the situation here. I am not rising to object to the building of the line to Willowbunch. I do not know whether it is really the right point or not. A great deal would depend on what is being done in the district. I have been told that the Canadian National has made an arrangement with the Canadian Pacific that the territory to the south and west will be looked after. We discussed in the House last year the question whether the line should be extended from Bengough in a westerly direction but a good deal more to the south than Willowbunch, Willowbunch being up a little to the north. Going down in that direction we run across a district where there are old, old settlers, who for years and years have had to haul their grain over distances which absolutely prevent any return. We have the Canadian Pacific line down there with quite a gap to be built, and there was a question I know as. to whether the Canadian Pacific would ever build that gap. Last year one
of the things we discussed was building down to the south and west for the purpose of relieving those people by an extension-I forget the meridian number at the moment, but I think it was No. 8. At any rate it would mean probably eighteen miles construction to the west of Bengough, reaching down to a country where there are any amount of people, and where they need the railway very badly. Now we are turning away from that and going up to Willowbunch, to the north and west, and I have been given to understand that the National thinks it will have discharged its duty to the people down there if it builds that way because an arrangement has been made with the Canadian Pacific to look after that other portion to the south. I really think the people of the district are entitled to have a clear statement as to that situation. Their necessities are great; the handicaps they have laboured under in the past are heavy, and this construction to Willowbunch rather looks as if for the future they had to depend on the Canadian Pacific.	I hope before this
conclusion has been come to that some arrangement has been made under which the Canadian Pacific will within a certain definite time make that other construction, and I would ask my hon. friend to let us know whether the Canadian Pacific is to build in that territory to the south and west, and if so, when that construction is going to be done.

The original idea of the
Canadian National was the line laid down in the bill now before the House. Last year a deviation was proposed, as my hon. friend says, in order to serve another part of the territory and, if I remember correctly, before the bill was through it was left quite optional as to different routes. Well, parliament has determined, and rightly so, that so far as possible there shall be little duplication.
We all agree on that.

Consequently it has been arranged, and I think the Canadian Pacific are perfectly agreeable, that while the Canadian National builds to Willowbunch the Canadian Pacific will build from the west. I am told but I am not sure-I have the papers somewhere and I think it Vas discussed in committee-that the Canadian Pacific has been getting out its charter and carrying out its surveys and will begin with the construction commencing not later than 1926.

Well, I have no doubt the district will be very glad to get
CJV.R.-Branch Lines

the assurance. I think they would like to see the work started this year; they have waited a tremendous time. I think the minister is fairly right in his discussion of the situation, except that he is wrong as to Willowbunch being the original proposition. What we had originally brought down last year was the building of a line from Radville. The Rad-ville line was a line considerably to the east of Bengough, and it ran through a very rough country where construction would be extremely heavy and where there were no settlers. It is true that when you got further south you encountered settlement; but you had to get away south before you met it and a lot of money would be lost in coming down that way. Before the Senate committee the engineers of the railway said they were always against the Radville line, they did not recommend it, and that the construction from Bengough would be more useful and more economical. Those are the only two propositions, whether the line is to go from Willow-bunch or Bengough. The alternative proposition last year was to extend for a longer distance to the south for the purpose of looking after those people who have been requiring attention for so many years. The action taken last year by this House was to leave it optional-whether the company would build from Radville south, or whether they would build from Bengough.

There is a question which occurred to me, not in direct connection with this bill but in connection with the construction of some branch lines: In the event of an agreement having been entered upon for the construction of a joint line, and a certain amount of money being put up by the Canadian National Railway and a certain amount on behalf of the Canadian Pacific, or some other company, who decides when the work must be gone on with? Has the government any power to compel the construction of the line?

That would not come up here. The only instance of an arrangement of this kind that I know of is the joint section which was to provide for the Drumheller district. That was agreed on yearn ago. I do not know how much of it has been constructed.
None.
I should have thought there was some.

If in order I should like to ask the minister for a moment to turn to this line-the Rosedale south east-
erly line. The money has been voted by this parliament, for the National's share and the Canadian Pacific has put up its portion. The officials of the latter company inform me they are ready to go on with the work, they are anxious to go on with it, but they cannot get the Canadian National to start the work. Who is to take the necessary action in a case of that kind? The people out there need the line, the people in Drumhdler need transportation facilities to move their coal; if the line were built it would mean a great deal more business for them in the district, and1 would also help the farmers along the route.
I sincerely hope that the minister will see that the Board of Railway Commissioners will take action in this regard. I cannot get satisfaction from anybody with respect to it.
Make application to the board.

I will take pleasure in
sending the remarks of my hon. friend to both the railway presidents to-morrow.
Send it to the Board of Railway Commissioners; that would be much better.

It is one of those difficult situations in regard to which I do not know where the authority lies unless it is with the Board of Railway Commissioners. I will see that the matter is brought to the attention of the company; it is the first I have heard of it. In a case of this kind we go to one company and of course they say they iare ready. Then we go to the other company and they say they are ready also; it is generally the other Miow that is delaying matters. The only thing is to try and get them to come together.

On section 2-Part of cost to be provided by Canadian Northern Railway Company and balance by Canadian National Railway Company; Canadian National may issjie security which may be guaranteed.

C.N.R-Branch Lines

In connection
with that I was going to ask my hon. friend how this is proposed to be taken into the company's capital? We may just as well be fair about this question, and look it straight in the face. This is our road and we are just as much liable for these bonds, endorsed as they are by the provincial treasurer, as we will be for the other bonds coming subsequently which we also have to endorse. Now what is to be done about it? Is there to be camouflage so that the obligation will not appear in the addition to the debt? Is there to be a statement made that we have not endorsed these bonds and therefore it should not come in as part of our obligations, or will the obvious, right thing be done in this one instance anyway? The people of Canada are building a railway with borrowed money. It is not enough to look after the whole of the line but we have to go out and borrow more. This loan which is a first charge upon that property is raised under the guarantee of the province. The next loan will have our guarantee on it, and surely it would be childish to pretend that that loan should, for the purpose of arriving at our own situation, be looked upon as anything other than our own obligation.
Well, I have not given it any thought, but this is cash we are getting.
I agree.
We are getting cash from the province. My own view absolutely, although on consideration I may be wrong, is that the Canadian National will be liable for the interest on the whole investment.

My hon. friend
does not quite catch my point. We are authorizing the government to guarantee further obligations because they will have to be issued in the name of the company. The security for those obligations is the line that is to be built. That security is subject to this cash as the minister points out. The cash does not make any difference one way or the other. What does count are the bonds already issued and guaranteed by the province: and before we can look to any of our security here at all if we are still foolish enough to go on thinking this railway is not ours, if we still go on hiding our heads in the sand and not looking upon an obligation of this character as an obligation of the whole country, then we are in the position of any second mortgagee. What is the good of a second mortgagee's security unless he is in a position to look after the first mortgage? I should have thought the thing was clear.

I did not expect a discussion of this kind, or I would have brushed up my memory a little. As a matter of fact, these branch lines of the Canadian Northern system are being treated I think in exactly the same way as they have been treated since the Canadian Northern was taken over by the government many years ago. The federal government I think paid the interest on these securities guaranteed by the provinces. I do not know whether the principal amounts were taken into the capital or not, but the principal amounts must be in the capital of the Canadian Northern system, because they are part of the Canadian Northern.
Sure.
And I imagine the capital charges will all be against some integral part of the Canadian National or Canadian Northern.
Sure. '

And the amount of interest due on all securities will appear in the books of the Canadian National. I understand they are a charge against the Canadian National, just as if they were part of the original account.

The minister is overlooking entirely the one thing of real importance here, and that is the question as to the government's investment and the question of the government's net or gross debt. If we are going on giving guarantees just as we feel like giving them, whether there are prior securities against the system or not, whether there is a value there on which we can get a return or not, then we are only misleading ourselves and misleading the public. The hon. minister says it is exactly the same as when the company owned it. Well, it ought not to be the same. So far as the coiftpany is concerned, it is the same, but I am speaking of the larger question, as to the government's position and the security for the people's money.

I will look into that
further. I had not given it any thought.

It occurs to me that
the Canadian National Railway is under some obligation to the people in that district in regard to this line. It must be remembered that in the vicinity of the Fife lake country and west of it, as far as the sixth and seventh meridian, or still further west-
I put it at the eighth meridian.

The eighth meridian
would be right-the people have for years been looking forward to the extension of the line from Bengough. At this time it appears as though an understanding had been reached between the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific Railways, and I should foe very glad if I thought such was the case. However, I am not assured of that. I 11 p.m. learned a few weeks ago that the Canadian Pacific Railway were proposing to introduce a bill in the upper chamber asking for authority to construct a road from south of Assiniboia and in the direction of Fife lake. I sent over to that chamber the other day for a copy of the bill, but I was informed there was no bill; so that I do not know whether the Canadian Pacific Railway is asking for that authority or not. I feel that the people in the Fife lake country and in the Wood mountain country will expect some assurance from the Canadian National that the Canadian Pacific is going to proceed with the development of our railway facilities in the south country. I want the minister to understand that I am not at all opposed to the extension of this line to Willowbuneh because I am familiar with the country, and I know that in the vicinity of Willowbuneh there is a splendid farming district. But I want to point out that if in the future it is necessary to extend the line from Willowbuneh to the westward, then the line should not really go down into the Willowbuneh valley, as I presume it is expected to do under this bill. The town of Willowbuneh lies in quite a deep valley, and it would seem that if the line were built into Willowbuneh it would probably remain a stub line for some time. The point I wish to make for the benefit of the minister is that there should be some assurance given to the people in that south country that railway facilities will foe developed either by the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific Railway. So far as I am concerned, I am not particular which line is built as long as the people in that country get the railway facilities. I wonder if the minister could give us some assurance in that regard.

I went over that ground
when the hon. member was not in the chamber. I pointed out that I felt confident that the Canadian Pacific Railway proposed to have an act of parliament passed to proceed with the surveys and begin construction from Assiniboia southward, not later, I think, than the year 1926.

South and east, if I remember. I do not think there is any question tha/t the Canadian Pacific intend doing that, and that arrangement having been arrived at, it would be unwise to duplicate lines. In the event of the
Canadian Pacific Railway proceeding with the programme which is apparently in prospect, it is not expected then to extend the line beyond Willowbuneh?
Not at the present time.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: The whole law is one of those inconvenient, troublesome things. What- the hon. member for Saskatoon says merely illustrates one of the annoyances of the act. The United States have no tax at all on cheques, and never have had. Great Britain first had a tax of a penny and afterwards made it two pence on all cheques, while we have all this nuisance of calculation and the like. I really think the character of the stamp is the least nuisance, because if you happen not to have a stamp you can attach a postage stamp lightly and the bank will always take it off >and substitute a proper stamp for it. I admit that it is a good thing to know what we are doing; I only wish we knew better what we are doing. Now under this section as we have it here- I have just seen it, but it strikes me offhand that it means that the broker not only passes on to his customer, the stamp taxes he pays to the bank, but he has to repeat the same proposition in connection with the same transaction.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I was going to ask the
minister in regard to the regulations under this act, I presume, calling for a stamp to be affixed to monthly statements sent out showing a previous payment. I think all who have to do with that class of business know that it is very difficult to send out statements without showing some payment if the account is not paid in full each month or at whatever interval it is rendered, and yet under this regulation it was necessary to affix 
a stamp according to the amount that was paid. There was an intimation-in fact, I think once it was dropped, then it was reinstated. Can the minister state whether that is to be dropped again?

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No, it will not be dropped.
My hon. friend was perhaps not in his seat when I explained a while ago that I had discussed this with the Deputy Minister of Customs and Excise who is administering the act, and he tells me that some firms were not issuing any receipt for moneys received on account during the month. The first of the month they send out a statement, and that constituted a receipt. I think my hon. friend will agree that they should pay, because it is a receipt. I will go a little further than I went a few minutes ago, and say that it is just possible that some firms doing business in an honest way may be penalized on account of the chaps who are evading the act, but I think the officers are trying to correct it as far as possible.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I appreciate the minister's difficulty. I am not bringing this forward to harass him in any way, or to be critical, but I have had a very large amount of correspondence from very reputable firms, as well as the Credit Mens' Association at Vancouver, and I presume other credit men's associations have also made similar representations. I appreciate it because I have had in years gone by a great deal of experience in this sort of thing. There are many concerns particularly wholesale houses, that carry accounts along year in and year out, which really are never closed. Perhaps there is a payment made on drafts, and so on, during the month, but they show at the end of the month that the business is not completed. Yet they are called upon under the new regulation to affix a stamp. Take the case that the minister mentioned. If a firm deliberately adopted the method of sending out statements yearly and not giving any receipt that would be easily distinguishable from the other class, and I submit this to the minister: It is hardly fair to penalize a score of honest, reputable firms because some one firm out of twenty, or perhaps one out of fifty, is seeking to evade the law in the way mentioned. I would rather see some regulation framed so that where it could be shown that they were evading the law they would be penalized rather than make such a sweeping general application. For all .the revenue the government gets out of the receipt tax I would suggest that that tax be abandoned altogether rather than cause this irritation and confusion.

Special War Revenue Act
I feel myself that the case made ;by these very numerous reputable firms-and I have in my room scores of letters on the subject-is one which the government should very carefully consider; and I would ask the minister if it is not still possible to at least drop this rather irritating regulation.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: The Minister of Customs and Excise is looking into the question now. I think the officials are trying to arrive at some method whereby a man who is doing business in an honest way will not be penalized.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: I wonder if my hon. friend could tell me exactly what that means? It is pretty hard to tell really what it means under this regulation. A receipt in the ordinary sense is an acquittance.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No, it might be a receipt on
k account.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Well, it is an
acquittance, it is pro tanto an acquittance. When you send a cheque in you get a receipt for your cheque; but on top of it you always have in every single course of business a monthly statement. That is the course followed by practically every wholesaler in the trade. Then, too, if there is a person that gets hit with the stamp tax it is the man that has an account with a broker. That happens all the time.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend but the statement of the broker is not taxed.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: Why is it not?

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have received a statement
every month and have not noticed any tax on it.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Now my hon.
friend is going to try and get that tax. Whenever I get a statement I notice there is an item charged for taxes.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: Of one sort or another.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Of one sort or
another. There is not a statement sent in but there is some charge for taxes.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We are talking of the stamp
tax now.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
So am I talking about the stamp tax. A charge is made for
the stamp tax some way or another.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
To what section is my
hon. friend referring.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
To the section
that refers to the stamping system. I really submit that we have gone just about far
enough in harassing the public. If we are to understand now that no one can get a statement of his account without paying a tax on that statement simply because there are some credit items in it I think the whole country ought to understand what is really being done. You cannot make a payment without paying a tax on your cheque; and for you to be told that you cannot get a statement of your account from your creditor without having to put more stamps on it, if that statement shows credit items, it does seem to be ridiculous. Yet that is what this section says.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: There is no change in the section.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I do not know
but the change comes in in this way. We have had sensible people administering this act at some times, and we have had other people administering the act at other times who I think are very far removed from that condition. We have had rulings that these statements ought not to be taxed, and we have had rulings that they are to be taxed. My hon. friend says it is his intention that the mere statement of account that a man gets from his creditor is to be stamped because there are credit items in it.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows better
than anyone in the House that the Department of Finance does not administer the act, although I am not shielding myself behind that statement at all. I have told the House frankly that I made inquiry of the deputy minister of the department administering the act and he explained to me that the reasons for the provision were that some people were evading the tax in the way mentioned. I agree with my hon. friend that if a remittance is made during the month, the person issuing the statement should not be compelled to put a stamp on his statement; but the Credit Men's Association should see to it that the merchants throughout the country, if they are members of their association, deal fairly with the department. The department must be protected in some way. Now if one person evades the law and my hon. friend does business fairly and rightly by issuing his. receipts and putting a stamp tax on them, does he not think it only is fair to him that everybody should be put on the same basis?

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I do not think the minister is putting everybody on the same basis. We have bad the illustration of a broker. Take the case of stocks that are held on margin with a broker and the dividend payments that are made by a company on its stock certificates. The debtor, who i3
Special War Revenue Act

carrying that stock, has not paid anything; he it not entitled to any receipt in one sense because he has paid no money. On the other hand the companies have paid their dividend cheques and have paid the stamp tax in every case. Does the minister really seriously say that all these little transactions should be segregated and the receipt stamp put on all of them?

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: No, what I say is that it has not been brought to my attention that the brokers do put stamps on their monthly statements. It is the first I have heard of it.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I know one
thing, and that is that when the business public really get to know how financing is going on in this country, they will transfer their transactions to the other side of the line. I wonder if the regulation is not driving business from Canada.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
In correcting evasions of the
law we are bringing business back.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: My hon. friend is not correcting it at all. If every time a statement is sent out for the payment of money it must have a stamp attached, simply because there are some credit items in that statement, it is about time we clearly understood the situation. If there is any one way of clearly showing the absurdity of the pyramiding of these little stamp taxes this certainly is the way.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I cannot agree with my
hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) in his attitude with regard to the stamp tax at all. The stamp tax is in essence a tax on a document evidencing a receipt of any description. If there is a receipt in the account, even should that money come from a third person, and it is credited to the person named in the account, why should the person not pay a stamp tax on that receipt, the same as on any other receipt?

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: Here we have a wholesaler distributing to a number of small retailers. A retailer comes in in the middle of the month and pays 850 on his account and gets a receipt, which is stamped. At the end of the month the wholesaler sends him a statement showing goods purchased to the value of S200. He has alreadjr paid the tax on the 850 he paid on the 14th of the month, and yet he is required to pay a tax again on the whole amount of his monthly statement, including the $50. The thing is preposterous.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is not the same
thing.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is what I am talking about.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is not the point raised by the hon. member for West York.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: He raised the same point in connection with a different class of receipt.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: No, not quite.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Let us stick to my point and see if we cannot win the minister to our view. I think the minister will admit, the government must admit, and every hon. member in the House must admit, that that is a gross injustice to that individual. Why persist in doing that? It is unquestionably a double tax. What will result is this: The wholesalers and others, in sending out their statements, when dealing with private families, where in many cases th'ey carry monthly accounts right along, will cease entering upon the statements the amounts paid, otherwise the stamp will have to be affixed, and while the sum may seem small, yet the accumulation of stamp taxes will amount to a great deal. There is a stamp tax on the cheques, and a stamp tax on the receiot, and a stamp tax on this, that and the other thing. It is multiplying the stamp taxes. That I think is really unreasonable. There may be one case in fifty where the department would lose money. I doubt if the minister or the department could cite in the whole of Canada half a dozen cases. They might possibly find half a dozen or a dozen, but supposing they found1 a hundred, that is nothing compared with the multiplicity of honest individuals who are going to be penalized. I say to the minister therefore that it is better to lose the small amount that is alleged to have been lost than to irritate and penalize the large number of honest dealers. I go a s'ep further still, and say that if it is found impossible to administer the stamp tax in an equitable fashion throughout the country, for the amount of revenue received it would be far better in the interests of harmony and keeping business in something like an equitable and favourable state of mind, to drop the whole thing. I do submit that that regulation should be withdrawn. I want to say to the minister, and through him to the department that administers these various taxes, that undoubtedly they have an irritating job. There is no question about it. The officials must be driven nearly to distraction, but there is always a tendency on the part of the official mind to disregard or overlook the convenience of the public, and to seek, and properly so, to exact the last dollar. That is where the minister ought to step in and j udge fairly between the public andl the

Special War Revenue Act
official honestly seeking to do his duty, it is true, but still perhaps erring a little too much in the matter of exactitude; so that I submit earnestly to the minister-and I hope he will take it up with his colleagues-that he should to-night give us an assurance that he will endeavour to have this regulation withdrawn. It is desirable, it is fair and it is equitable to withdraw it; on the other hand, to enforce it is going to do more injury to honest and reputable firms than the value of the revenue received would warrant.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: In the absence of the minister who is administering the act, I cannot agree to have it withdrawn. I will take it up with him once again and see if it cannot be arranged. I am sure the government is desirous of avoiding irritation.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
What the hon. member.
(Mr. Stevens) asks for can be done by regulation. He is simply desirous of avoiding paying the double tax. He does not want to attach a stamp to a monthly statement, but does not object to attaching a stamp to the ordinary receipt.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: No.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: Where the money is paid during the currency of the account, my hon. friend would object to the provision that a stamp should be attached to the statement; but that is a matter which can be arranged by regulation.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is the matter we are complaining of, and the difficulty is we cannot deal with it in the act because it is in the regulation.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: I have just heard a part of the discussion, and I realize from the discussion that a letter I received from a friend who is doing a very large retail business in St. John is not without foundation. I presumed when I got the letter that there must be some extraordinary mistake, because what he complained of was that where a partial payment had been made, possibly by cheque- but that would not matter-he had to give a receipt duly stamped; and that if he sent out an ordinary monthly statement of account afterwards showing the credit that had been received,, he must place a stamp on that. Surely that cannot be the regulation. It must be a misinterpretation of the spirit of the act.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is the regulation.

maintopic: THE SPECIAL WAR REVENUE ACT, 1915 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If that is 'the regulation,
with all respect to the gentleman who framed it, it seems to me profoundly absurd and unjust, and I trust the minister will find some way to remedy it. As far as any possible
chance of evasion or fraud is concerned, I agree with hon. members who have stated that it must be almost infinitesimal. The minister himself in this very bill is opening to my mind a far greater chance of loss, because while firms such as the one I am speaking of will not resort to it, there are many individuals who will resort to the expedient of issuing a large number of cheques just under the sum of $5, in order to pay an account which amounts to much more than 15. In fact, I cannot understand opening a door such ajs is opened by this act, because it leaves it open to them to evade the tax, not by fraud, but by an absolute compliance with the act, which will militate against the stamp tax revenue which the government has a right to expect. I do not care whether you place the amount at $5, $10, or $25 there will always be an opportunity for evasion, so long as the sum owed is greater than the amount fixed by the act. It is a door which should not be opened. I sympathize with the people who dislike putting a stamp on a three or four dollar cheque, but surely there should be no need to trouble the House with a discussion of this matter at all. This stamp tax has been so long in force in England that it should be decided to adopt the experience of a half century at least or perhaps more. People have practised every trick of evasion, and they have met them where it was necessary to meet them. To follow them I think would be reasonable, but to try to provide for every possible case where there may be some peculiarity of the human mind looking for an evasion only results in intolerable torment and burdensomeness to people who are honestly trying to comply with the law, but do not want to be dealt with unjustly. Ail these matters are unfortunate. The conditions which make the stamp tax necessary are unfortunate. 'Surely we should be able to collect the tax with as little friction as possible, but we should not exact the taxes in such a way that people feel they are paying more than one tax for one transaction. That arouses a feeling of injustice which is not easily quelled. It causes discontent with taxation in general, and I think that our office as legislators ought to be directed to making taxation ias palatable as possible and to create, if we can in the public mind the idea that the people should loyally and if possible cheerfully accept the burdens of taxation. You cannot get that feeling when a man sees that he is discriminated against with absolute, implacable injustice.
